187	## 5. The inbound path
188	
189	**One HTTP request becomes one Postgres transaction**, with no network call
190	inside it and no background step. Appendix C.3 has the sequence: validate, claim
191	the `eventId`, lock the record, then four steps per field, then commit and 200.
192	
193	- **(a) learn** records what Salesforce holds regardless of what (c) decides,
194	  which is what collapses repair into the single condition 8.3.
195	- **(b) restatement** skips a field restating the `sf_value` we already held (8.4).
196	- **(c) decide** takes the first case that applies — echo, value-already-equal
197	  (`confirmed`), the order-key comparison, `superseded` — and only here can a
198	  current value change.
199	- **(d) repair** is condition 8.3, after every field whatever happened to it.
200	
201	**The duplicate claim and the apply share one transaction:** split them and a
202	crash between marks an event processed that was never applied, which Salesforce
203	will never resend. **Fields are independent**, so one event may apply `phone` and
204	supersede `city`, making the event's outcome `partial`.
205	
206	> A change whose canonical value already equals the current value changes
207	> **nothing** — not the value, not the order key, and not history.
208	
209	| Resolving the record | Rule |
210	| --- | --- |
211	| **(a)** known `sf_id` | one indexed lookup, lock, proceed |
212	| **(b)** unknown `sf_id`, human `changedBy` | mint a `portal_id`, insert link and empty row, apply every field as a first write. **Recovery (10.3) reuses this** |
213	| **(c)** unknown `sf_id`, integration user | the echo of a create *we* made. **503 + `Retry-After: 5`, apply nothing**; by redelivery it is case (a). After 60 s, log loudly and treat as (b) |
214	
215	**400 versus 500**, since a 400 discards the event forever: an unknown *field
216	name* earns one; a *value* we failed to canonicalise is our bug and earns a 500.
217	
218	## 6. The outbound path
219	
220	**6.1 The portal save.** The handler takes part 5's record lock, stamps
221	`occurred_at` from `clock_timestamp()` and the actor from the session (A9), calls
222	`applyChanges`, and commits — **the value change and the queue row are the same
223	commit**, created by **condition 8.3, as on the inbound path**.
224	
225	**6.2 The worker loop** (Appendix C.4). Each tick: hold the leader lease (else
226	idle as a standby, [ADR 0003](adr/0003-one-sender-with-a-leader-lease.md));
227	reclaim rows whose 30-second lease expired; probe instead of claiming if the
228	breaker is open; claim **whole records**, oldest-due first so nothing starves;
229	read current values and build one call per record; take a governor token; send
230	and settle. `attempts` rises when a row is **claimed**, not when it fails, so a
231	row that crashes us mid-send cannot be retried forever.
232	
233	**6.3 Coalescing, and reading the value late.** All fields owed on one record
234	become **one** call — a four-field form save is four rows and one PATCH.
235	
236	> The sender reads each field's **current value at send time**, never a value
237	> carried on the queue row, which is why part 4 stores none.
238	
239	A city edit at 09:00 and another at 11:00 during an outage therefore send **the
240	11:00 value, once.** On a `2xx`, **after** the response and never before, the
241	sender sets `sf_value` to what it sent, writes the `echo_fence` rows, and records
242	`sent_at` (Appendix B traces the divergence that first step prevents).
243	
244	**6.4 The cap, slowing down, and the breaker. 70 of the 100 req/s,** both bounds
245	chosen. *Not 100:* the cap counts our retries and belongs to the client's org, so
246	another integration's burst would reach us as rejections, while at 70 a 30% burst
247	is absorbed. *Not lower:* catch-up scales inversely — 10.4 row 1 drains in
248	6.3 min, row 5 at a governor of 25 takes 16.0. Steady state spends ~7.4 req/s, so
249	we run at **11% utilisation** and the other 89% drains backlogs.
250	
251	On a slow-down signal (A8), nothing is dropped:
252	
253	```
254	rate := max(5, rate / 2)                   -- multiplicative decrease
255	row.state := 'pending'
256	row.next_attempt_at := now + (Retry-After, else 2^attempts s jittered, cap 300 s)
257	row.attempts := attempts - 1               -- given back: not the row's fault
258	recover: rate := min(70, rate + 5) per 30 s of clean responses
259	```
260	
261	**The breaker splits two failures, and that split is what makes a 6-hour outage
262	survivable.** An **endpoint failure** (refused, timeout, 5xx) says nothing about
263	the row: after 5 consecutive ones we stop claiming and probe every 30 s, and
264	claimed rows return to `pending` **with attempts restored**. A **row failure**, a
265	400-class rejection naming this record's data, is the only kind counting attempts
266	toward giving up (F.6).
267	
268	**6.5 Restart, and settling a group.** A restart is a non-event: the new process
269	takes the lease, reclaims expired rows, and resumes; a row that reached
270	Salesforce before the crash is sent again, safely, because all three calls are
271	idempotent (C.1).
272	
273	| Outcome | State | Attempts | Then |
274	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
275	| `2xx` | `sent` | — | set `sf_value`/`sf_observed_at`; write `echo_fence`; record `sent_at` |
276	| `429` / limit | `pending` | restored | halve the rate; honour `Retry-After` |
277	| timeout / refused / `5xx` | `pending` | restored | counts toward the breaker; backoff with jitter |
278	| `400`-class, data rejected | `failed` | kept | **alert** — a value we accept and Salesforce refuses needs a human |
279	| `404`, record gone | `failed` | kept | **alert** — deletes are out of scope (A15) |
280	| `401` / `403` | `pending` | restored | **page, stop the sender** — else the queue burns into `failed` |
281	
282	A `failed` row is never deleted; it keeps its `last_error`.
283	
284	## 7. The rule when both sides change the same record
285	
286	**7.1 Who is doing the merging.** **Salesforce has no merge logic**, so our
287	database holds the decision — and hence the rule that is easy to miss: **a
288	webhook we reject is not a no-op.** It is the discovery that Salesforce holds a
289	value we rejected, and it owes an outbound call (8.3).
290	
291	**7.2 The order key — the field that decides which edit is current.**
292	
293	| Component | On a webhook | On a portal save |
294	| --- | --- | --- |
295	| `occurred_at` | **the payload's `occurredAt`** | **`clock_timestamp()` of the saving transaction** (A9) |
296	| `origin_rank` | `1` | `0` |
297	| `origin_event_id` | **the payload's `eventId`** | the portal change id, a ULID per save |
298	
299	> **Apply the incoming change if and only if its order key is strictly greater
300	> than the stored one.**
301	
302	`clock_timestamp()`, not `now()`, which returns the transaction's start. On an
303	exact tie **Salesforce wins**, the cheaper direction; a shared millisecond (A11)
304	breaks on `origin_event_id`, arbitrarily but **stably**. Strictness is
305	load-bearing: `>` and not `>=` makes re-applying an applied change a no-op (F.7).
306	
307	**7.3 Canonical form.** Canonicalised **before** being compared or stored; the
308	stored form is canonical.
309	
310	| Field | Canonical form |
311	| --- | --- |
312	| all text | Unicode NFC; trim; collapse internal whitespace runs to one space |
313	| `email` | the above, then lowercased whole |
314	| `phone` | E.164 by the contact's country; on a parse failure, digits with a leading `+`, and count it |
315	| `status` | mapped through the agreed picklist vocabulary |
316	| `customer_id` | the `portal_id` UUID, lowercase hex |
317	| empty | `''` and `NULL` are one thing, stored `NULL` |
318	
319	Not hygiene — this is what makes part 9 true: **one formatting difference reads as
320	a change and turns the sync into a generator of its own traffic** (F.7).
321	
322	**7.4 Different fields — the brief's own scenario.** No conflict rule needed,
323	which is the argument for ADR 0002: finance sets `city`, then sales changes
324	`phone` and the webhook names `phone` only (A3), so `city` is never looked at.
325	The portal ends with the new phone **and** the finance city, each with its own
326	actor and time (Appendix A).
327	
328	**7.5 The same field. Across the two sides:** the order key decides; the winner
329	gets an `applied` row; **the loser is kept** as `superseded` with its value, actor
330	and time (the brief is explicit that an earlier edit stays on record); and **if
331	the loser was Salesforce's value, a repair write is enqueued** (8.3). **Two
332	portal users:** the record lock serialises the saves rather than tying them, so
333	the second wins on a later `clock_timestamp()` and the first's value survives in
334	`field_change` under their name. What they *see* is a product decision (open
335	question 4); my rule is that the portal renders each field as "set by X at T" and
336	names who replaced a submitted value — **no blocking, no merge dialog.**
337	
338	**7.6 Two clocks: the rule for the skew window.** 7.2 compares Salesforce's clock
339	against ours, so inside the skew window (A10: 2 s) an edit made second can rank
340	first.
341	
342	> **The order key stays authoritative inside the window; we do not detect or
343	> correct an inversion. We bound the skew, and we measure and page on the
344	> inversions.**
345	
346	| | |
347	| --- | --- |
348	| **Bound** | hosts run NTP; drift above **500 ms** is a host alarm, so at most a quarter of A10's 2 s is ours |
349	| **Measure** | **cross-side near-tie inversions/hour**: `superseded` rows whose superseding change has the opposite `origin` and `abs(Δ occurred_at) ≤ 2 s` |
350	| **Warn / page** | 5/hour; **20/hour**, or a rolling 4-hour window where **≥ 80%** of inversions favour one origin |
351	
352	The bias threshold does the work: genuine races go both ways, so a sustained
353	one-directional result is the signature of real skew. **No deterministic in-window
354	tiebreak is offered** (F.7).
355	
356	## 8. Duplicates and out-of-order changes
357	
358	**8.1 A duplicate webhook. `eventId` is the idempotency key, claimed in the same
359	transaction as the apply.** No row from the `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` means we have
360	seen it: commit, answer `200 {"status":"duplicate"}`, change nothing. Salesforce
361	has done nothing wrong (A7), so this is counted, not alerted. Two independent
362	layers, **and only the second is the guarantee:** *suppression*, the table, so a
363	duplicate does no work; and *harmlessness*, the strict `>` of 7.2, which makes an
364	unsuppressed duplicate a no-op anyway — the table falls to a prune or a truncate,
365	the compare holds regardless (F.8). A repeated `eventId` carrying a *different*
366	`payload_hash` is a provider bug: first write wins, and this one **is** alerted.
367	
368	**8.2 An older webhook after a newer one.**
369	
370	> **Compare order keys per field; a change not strictly newer never becomes
371	> current, and is recorded `superseded`.**
372	
373	```
374	evt_A  phone -> ...0001  occurredAt 11:30:04.000    evt_B  phone -> ...0002  11:30:09.000
375	
376	B first:  11:30:09 > stored           -> APPLIED. current ...0002,
377	                                         sf_value ...0002, sf_observed_at 11:30:09
378	A second: (a) 11:30:04 NOT > 11:30:09 -> sf_value LEFT ALONE (a later SF state is known)
379	          (c) 11:30:04 < 11:30:09     -> SUPERSEDED. history keeps ...0001,
380	                                         sales.user, 11:30:04; current stays ...0002
381	          (d) sf_value = current      -> NO repair write
382	```
383	
384	Step (a) is what makes this correct rather than merely plausible: `evt_A`
385	describes a **past** state of Salesforce, so `sf_value` must not move. **No
386	reordering buffer** — A11 gives no sequence numbers, so we cannot detect that
387	anything is *missing* (F.8).
388	
389	**8.3 The repair write — one condition for every case.**
390	
391	> **After every field, regardless of what happened to it: if
392	> `field_version.sf_value` is distinct from the current value, enqueue a repair
393	> write.**
394	
395	"Distinct from" is SQL's `IS DISTINCT FROM`, and the NULL case is load-bearing:
396	**an `sf_value` we have never learned is distinct from any current value.**
397	Without it every portal-created record would be stranded.
398	
399	| What happened | `sf_value` after | Current | Repair? |
400	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
401	| Salesforce change applied | the new value | the same | no |
402	| Salesforce value superseded by a newer portal edit | Salesforce's | ours | **yes** |
403	| older event after a newer one (8.2) | unchanged | matches it | no |
404	| echo of our own write | what we sent | the same | no |
405	| Salesforce restates a value we hold | that value | the same | no |
406	| full-record restatement during an outage (8.4) | Salesforce's stale value | our unsent edit | **yes** |
407	
408	It **terminates** — the repair sends our current value, the echo sets `sf_value`
409	to it, the condition goes false — and it is the **entire logic of outage
410	recovery** (10.3).
411	
412	**8.4 If a webhook carries the full record instead.** A3 assumes
413	changed-fields-only, and **full-record mode is the dangerous one**, because a
414	field's silence and its restatement look identical. *The hazard:* finance sets
415	`city` to Noida at 15:00, unsent; at 16:00 a sales user changes the phone and the
416	full-record payload restates `city: "Gurugram"`, stamped 16:00. Compared as a
417	change, `16:00 > 15:00`, so we would **overwrite the finance edit with an older
418	value Salesforce was merely restating.**
419	
420	> *The rule,* step (b) of the apply: **a field whose canonical value equals the
421	> `sf_value` we already held is a restatement — not restamped, not compared, not
422	> touched.**
423	
424	Traced: `sf_value[city]` is already `Gurugram`, so `city` is skipped and stays
425	Noida while 8.3 enqueues the repair we already owed; `phone` differs and applies
426	normally. **Step (b) is unconditional**, whatever the payload shape, which is why
427	`applyChanges` needs no mode parameter — and the outage sweep (10.3) requires it
428	regardless.
429	
430	## 9. The rule that stops a loop
431	
432	Ranked second of eight: a loop consumes the whole 100 req/s budget and stops sync
433	for every record at once, within seconds of deployment.
434	
435	> **9.1 — L1, the structural rule.** Outbound work is created exactly when
436	> `field_version.sf_value` differs from a field's current value — condition 8.3,
437	> after every field, on both paths, and nowhere else.
438	
439	```
440	portal sets city = Noida  -> sf_value "Gurugram" <> "Noida"  -> 1 outbound row
441	we PATCH Noida, 2xx       -> sf_value := "Noida"                            (6.3)
442	Salesforce echoes Noida   -> sf_value "Noida" = current       -> 0 rows.  Dead.
443	```
444	
445	No fuel after one hop, because there is nothing left to disagree about.
446	**Precondition: canonical form (7.3).**
447	
448	> **9.2 — L2, the actor rule.** A webhook whose `changedBy` is the integration user
449	> (A6) is an echo: recorded, never compared, never applied.
450	
451	L1 guarantees the loop stops; L2 that it stops on the **right value**, since an
452	echo carries a later time than the edit our write overwrote and would otherwise
453	launder a stale value over a newer one (Appendix B).
454	
455	> **9.3 — L3, the echo fence.** After a 2xx the sender records the record, field and
456	> hash of the canonical value sent, expiring in 15 minutes; an inbound change
457	> matching an unexpired entry is an echo.
458	
459	> **9.4 — L4, the repair breaker.** Above **5 repairs to one field in an hour**,
460	> enqueue nothing more for it, mark it contested, and alert.
461	
462	L3 is L2's guarantee keyed on the value rather than the actor, so it holds if A6
463	is false. L4 bounds the one way L1 fails: a spelling our canonical form does not
464	normalise makes every echo read as disagreement.
465	
466	| | Guarantees | Absent |
467	| --- | --- | --- |
468	| **L1** + canonical form | the loop **terminates** | everything; no other layer saves us |
469	| **L2** | it terminates on the **right value** | our own write launders a stale value over a newer one |
470	| L3 | L2's guarantee without A6 | nothing, while A6 holds |
471	| L4 | bounds L1's one failure mode | an unbounded argument over one field |
472	
473	## 10. The 6-hour outage
474	
475	**10.1 What it is.** Six hours with the Salesforce API unreachable and webhooks
476	sent during it possibly never arriving — dark both ways at once (A16).
477	
478	**The arithmetic uses the business-hours average of 3 edits/s, not A1's 20/s
479	peak.** Saying so up front because the two differ greatly — about 6 minutes
480	against about 35 — and the choice is a judgement, not an oversight: a peak is a
481	15-minute phenomenon, and six consecutive hours of one is not credible. The peak
482	is carried as row 3 of 10.4, so both numbers are on the page. **The portal keeps
483	working throughout:** edits apply locally and queue for Salesforce, so the only
484	cost is visibility there, and the 30-second target does not apply during catch-up.
485	
486	**10.2 What is on disk.**
487	
488	| | At the worst moment | Why |
489	| --- | --- | --- |
490	| `outbound_change`, `pending` | **19,440 rows, ~4.9 MB** | each committed with the edit that caused it (6.1) |
491	| rows left `inflight` by a restart | a handful | reclaimed when the 30-second lease expires |
492	| `sync_watermark` | one row per object type | where the sweep resumes |
493	
494	Five megabytes is what "pending calls must still be there after our process
495	restarts" costs, and **a restart during the outage is a non-event.**
496	
497	**10.3 How we drain it — and why the order is not negotiable.**
498	
499	> **The inbound sweep must complete before the outbound drain begins.**
500	
501	The loss it prevents: finance sets a city to Noida at 15:00, queued unsent; at
502	17:00 a sales user sets it to Delhi in Salesforce and that webhook never arrives.
503	*Drain first:* we PATCH Noida, Delhi is overwritten, and the sweep reads back our
504	own value — **Delhi is destroyed with no record it existed.** *Sweep first:*
505	Delhi's 17:00 `SystemModstamp` beats the portal's 15:00, Noida is kept as
506	`superseded` under the finance user's name, and the queued row then sends the
507	**current** value (6.3) — Delhi, a no-op.
508	
509	With 14,954 portal-touched and 34,892 Salesforce-touched records out of 5 M
510	(row 1), the expected overlap is `14,954 × 34,892 / 5,000,000` = **104 records**,
511	and the ordering costs no time. **The sweep also depends on the restatement rule
512	(8.4)**, since a `SystemModstamp` is a *record's* time, so a record touched at
513	17:00 hands back every field stamped 17:00. Appendix C.5 has the sequence: probe,
514	hold the drain, page through the changed-since query feeding each record in as a
515	full-record observation, advance the watermark per page, release at half rate.
516	
517	**10.4 The arithmetic — every figure, in one table.** Every number in this
518	document comes out of these lines; the table varies one assumption per row.
519	
520	```
521	window           6 h x 3600                                 = 21,600 s
522	queued changes   portal edits/s x 21,600
523	outbound calls   queued changes / 1.3 changes per record      (coalescing, 6.3)
524	drain capacity   governor - 7.4 req/s reserved for live traffic
525	                 (7.4 = peak steady state: (6 + 0.7 repairs) x 1.1 retries, 6.4)
526	drain            resume at half the governor, +5 req/s every 30 s, then full
527	sweep            Salesforce records / 2,000 per SOQL page     (requests)
528	                 Salesforce records / 500 per second          (local apply)
529	total            sweep + drain  -- the sweep blocks the drain (10.3)
530	```
531	
532	| # | Scenario | What varies | portal /s | queued | calls | drain | SF records | reqs | sweep | **total** |
533	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
534	| **1** | **base** | — | 0.90 | 19,440 | 14,954 | 5.1 | 34,892 | 18 | 1.2 | **6.3** |
535	| 2 | no coalescing | 1.0 chg/rec | 0.90 | 19,440 | 19,440 | 6.3 | 34,892 | 18 | 1.2 | **7.5** |
536	| 3 | sustained peak | A1 → 20/s | 6.00 | 129,600 | 99,692 | 27.7 | 232,615 | 117 | 7.8 | **35.4** |
537	| 4 | portal-heavy | A2 → 70% portal | 2.10 | 45,360 | 34,892 | 12.0 | 14,954 | 8 | 0.5 | **12.5** |
538	| 5 | contended cap | A12 → governor 25 | 0.90 | 19,440 | 14,954 | 14.8 | 34,892 | 18 | 1.2 | **16.0** |
539	| 6 | no changed-since | A4 false → all 5 M | 0.90 | 19,440 | 14,954 | 5.1 | 5,000,000 | 2,500 | 16.7 | **21.8** |
540	
541	Drain, sweep and total are minutes. **Row 1 is the answer: about 6 minutes.**
542	
543	```
544	Row 1, with the division shown
545	queued     0.9 x 21,600                             = 19,440 changes
546	calls      19,440 / 1.3                             = 14,954
547	capacity   70 - 7.4                                 = 62.6 req/s at full rate
548	ramp       35,40,45,50,55,60,65 req/s, 30 s each, each minus 7.4:
549	           (27.6+32.6+37.6+42.6+47.6+52.6+57.6) x 30 = 8,946 calls in 210 s
550	rest       (14,954 - 8,946) / 62.6                  = 96.0 s
551	drain      210 + 96.0 = 306.0 s                     = 5.1 minutes
552	sweep      2.1 x 21,600 / 1.3                       = 34,892 records
553	           34,892 / 2,000 = 18 requests (0.3 s of budget)
554	           34,892 / 500   = 69.8 s                  = 1.2 minutes
555	TOTAL      1.2 + 5.1                                = 6.3 minutes
556	```
557	
558	Allow **under 10 minutes** operationally, covering page-fetch latency, retries,
559	and the breaker needing a few probes to close. **Beyond row 1:** the **cap is the
560	floor, not our design** — row 3 at the full 100 req/s with no reserve is still
561	`99,692 / 100 = 997 s = 16.6 min`, so our 30% reserve costs ~11 minutes in the
562	worst credible case (A12). **Row 6 demotes A4** from load-bearing to preferable,
563	and I would run that sweep **nightly regardless**, as the standing net under lost
564	webhooks, canonicalisation gaps, fields L4 gave up on, and 7.6's inversions.
565	
566	## 11. Three numbers I would watch
567	
568	One per failure mode: outbound stuck, inbound slow, and getting it wrong. The
569	third is the only one that detects incorrectness rather than slowness.
570	
571	| | Number | Normal | Warn | **Call someone** |
572	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
573	| **1** | **age of the oldest unsent change** — `min(created_at)` over `pending` | < 5 s | 60 s | **300 s (5 min)** |
574	| **2** | **inbound lag** — p99 `applied_at − occurred_at`, Salesforce-origin, last 5 min | < 6 s | 20 s | **> 30 s for 5 min** |
575	| **3** | **divergence** — repairs + Salesforce-origin `superseded` per minute; **and** 7.6's inversions per hour | ~0; < 1/h | 10/min; 5/h | **100/min; 20/h; or ≥ 80% one-way over 4 h** |
576	
577	**Age, not depth,** for number 1: 19,000 rows draining fast is healthy, 3 rows
578	stuck is not. Number 2 **includes Salesforce's own emission delay**, because the
579	30 seconds we promised is end to end. Number 3 is the only one that reports a skew
580	past A10, a canonicalisation gap, or a loop rule that stopped working. **On the
581	dashboard but not paging:** the governor's rate and 429 count, the breaker's
582	state, rows in `failed` and fields marked contested, signature failures and 400s,
583	and `sync_watermark` lag.
584	
585	## 12. What I am leaving out
586	
587	**Because the exercise says so:** deletes (A15), Salesforce login screens, any
588	visual UI, a second region, and load testing real Salesforce. Where code exists
589	it runs against a fake Salesforce I wrote.
590	
591	**Because I chose to:** the **initial 5 M backfill** (S8, costed as row 6 of
592	10.4); **Salesforce auth lifecycle** (mechanical); **schema-change handling** (L4
593	degrades an unknown picklist value into a contested field, not a loop);
594	**merging already-duplicated records** (a pre-existing data-quality problem);
595	**field-level permissions** (open question 6); **objects and fields beyond the
596	nine** (A14); **the portal's overwrite notice** (7.5's rule is designed, the UI
597	is not); **right-to-erasure against permanent history** (open question 5); and
598	**the monitoring plumbing** (part 11 has the queries).
599	
600	**What I would build first:** S1 and S2 alone for a week — the merge rule, the
601	history, canonical form, and the one condition — against a fake Salesforce;
602	everything after is plumbing around a decision that has to be right first. And I
603	would get open question 1 answered first: Change Data Capture replay ids would
604	retire A11, strengthen 8.2 from ordering-what-arrived to detecting-what-is-missing,
605	and turn the recovery sweep into a replay.
606

# Two-way sync of customer and contact records

**Design document — Tequity Round 1**

Sales edits customers and contacts in Salesforce; finance and customer-success
edit the same records in the portal Tequity built on Postgres. Both copies must
agree within 30 seconds while both are up, every field's history must be kept,
and we control only our side.

Parts 7–10 are the four rules; all arithmetic is one table in 10.4. Every
justification lives in [`design-appendix.md`](design-appendix.md) (**F**, by
section), with the brief's scenario and the hardest race traced (**A**, **B**),
interfaces, schema DDL and sequences (**C**), the assumptions derived (**D**),
and what the demo substitutes for (**E**). `docs/adr/` holds the three decisions
expensive to reverse.

## Summary

The unit of sync is a **field**, not a record. Each field carries an **order key**
`(occurred_at, origin_rank, origin_event_id)`; the current value is the one whose
key is greatest. **Salesforce has no merge logic** — it overwrites with whatever
lands last — so our database holds the decision and Salesforce's copy is a
projection of it. Hence the one rule everything follows from:

> **Outbound work is created exactly when `sf_value` — what we believe Salesforce
> holds for a field — differs from that field's current value.** After every
> field, on both paths, nowhere else.
> *We call Salesforce when, and only when, we believe Salesforce disagrees with us.*

| Rule | | § |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Duplicate** | `eventId` claimed in the apply's transaction; and `>` is strict, so an escaped duplicate is a no-op | 8.1 |
| **Out of order** | order keys per field; not-newer never becomes current, kept as `superseded` with actor and time | 8.2 |
| **Loop** | an echo makes `sf_value` equal the current value, so the condition goes false — no fuel after one hop | 9 |
| **6-h outage** | queue rows commit with the edit; on recovery the sweep runs **before** the drain | 10.3 |

**Numbers.** Peak 20 edits/s assumed, business-hours average 3, quiet hour 0.5.
We run at **70 of the 100 req/s** allowed, 11% used in steady state. A 6-hour
outage queues **19,440 changes → 14,954 calls**, draining in 5.1 min; with the
1.2-min sweep first, **6.3 min** (row 1, 10.4). The 30-second target closes at
~6 s both ways, 7 of the 9.8 worst-case seconds being Salesforce's.

## 1. Assumptions, and the questions I would ask

Nothing below was given; **Appendix D derives each and says what changes if it
goes the other way.** The exercise names five — A1, A3, A4, A7, A9 — and **A4 and
A5 assume Salesforce APIs the brief does not mention.**

| | Assumption |
| --- | --- |
| **A1** | **Peak 20 edits/s, business-hours average 3/s, quiet 0.5/s.** 10.4 uses the average; 10.1 says why |
| **A2** | 70% of edits originate in Salesforce, 30% in the portal |
| **A3** | **A webhook carries only the changed fields**, per the sample |
| **A4** | **Salesforce can be queried for records changed in a window** (SOQL on `SystemModstamp`, 2,000/page). **Assumed** |
| **A5** | **Creates can be made idempotent** by external-id upsert on our `portalId`. **Assumed** |
| **A6** | `changedBy` names the API caller, so our integration user is recognisable |
| **A7** | **Delivery is at-least-once**; HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body; retried on 5xx or timeout |
| **A8** | Throttling arrives as 429 or `REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`, with `Retry-After` when available |
| **A9** | **A portal save takes its time from our `clock_timestamp()` and its actor from the session** — never the body's `editedBy` |
| **A10** | Clock skew between the two clocks is at most 2 s |
| **A11** | `occurredAt` is UTC, millisecond; two edits can share a millisecond |
| **A12** | The 100 req/s cap is ours alone to spend, and **we run at 70** |
| **A13** | Salesforce emits within 5 s p99; a record write returns within 2 s p99 |
| **A14** | The nine named fields are the whole schema |
| **A15** | No record is ever deleted (the exercise's scope) |
| **A16** | **The outage is dark both ways at once** — the harder reading of the brief |

**Questions I could not close with an assumption.** (1) **How is the webhook
produced** — Apex callout, Platform Event, Change Data Capture, middleware? It
decides A4, A6 and A11 together; highest-value question here. (2) Is there an
external-id field on Account and Contact we may write (A5)? (3) What else in the
org spends the API limit (A12; row 5, 10.4)? (4) When two portal users edit one
field, what should the second see? 7.5 is my rule, but the choice is a product
decision. (5) Must history be retained legally, and does that conflict with
right-to-erasure? Part 4 never deletes a change. (6) Is any field single-owner?
I assume not; if some are, we need a per-field ownership table.

## 2. The systems, who calls whom, the network seam, the interfaces

```
 sales user              finance / customer-success user
     | edits in                      | edits in
     v                               v
+--------------+         +--------------------+
|  SALESFORCE  |         |  TEQUITY PORTAL    |
| their CRM+DB |         |  our app           |
+--------------+         +--------------------+
   |      ^                     | in-process
   |      |                     v
   |      |   +-----------------------------------+
   |      |   | MERGE   order keys, history, echo |
   |      |   |         and repair decisions      |
   |      |   +-----------------------------------+
   |      |          |                   ^
   |      |          v                   |
   |      |   +-----------------------------------+
   |      |   | POSTGRES  records, history, queue |
   |      |   +-----------------------------------+
   |      |         ^                     |
   | == PUBLIC INTERNET == only path      v
   |      | (A) SF->us            +-----------------+
   +------|---------> [EP] -------| SYNC WORKER     |
          | (B) us->SF            | governor, sweep |
          +-----------------------+-----------------+
            record API: create / update / changed-since

 [EP] WEBHOOK ENDPOINT (ours): validate, dedupe, MERGE, commit, 200.
```

| Path | Caller | Callee | Trigger | Cap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A** | Salesforce | our webhook endpoint | a record changed in Salesforce | none; inbound is outside the cap |
| **B** | our sync worker | Salesforce record API | we believe Salesforce disagrees | 100 req/s hard; we run at 70 |
| — | the portal's save handler | MERGE, in-process | a portal user saved | not a network call |

No human crosses the internet seam; only paths A and B do. **Two processes, one
repository, and the seam between them is Postgres** — not HTTP, not a broker
([ADR 0001](adr/0001-two-processes-with-postgres-as-the-seam.md)) — so the
inbound apply and the outbound enqueue are **one commit**.

| Crosses the boundary | Written by | Read by | Means |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `outbound_change` | endpoint and portal, in the merge transaction | sync worker | "Salesforce disagrees about this field" |
| `echo_fence` | sync worker, after a successful send | endpoint | "we just wrote this; expect it back" |

**Appendix C.1 has the interface on each side**: our endpoint's contract and
status codes, the three Salesforce operations we depend on — each idempotent **by
design**, which is what makes at-least-once sending safe — and `applyChanges`.

**Does 30 seconds close?** Yes, at ~6 s both ways:

| Portal → Salesforce | p99 | Salesforce → portal | p99 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| commit (queue row is in it) | — | Salesforce emits (A13, **not ours**) | 5.0 s |
| worker notices (`NOTIFY`, 1 s poll) | 1.0 s | network | 0.5 s |
| coalescing window | 1.0 s | our apply transaction | 0.2 s |
| queue wait at 11% utilisation | 0.1 s | | |
| Salesforce write (A13, **not ours**) | 2.0 s | | |
| **total** | **4.1 s** | **total** | **5.7 s** |

**No inbound queue** — at A1's peak the endpoint commits 14 transactions a second.

## 3. The subproblems, in the order I would build them

**Ordered by risk:** (1) getting it wrong loses data unrecoverably, (2) getting
it wrong is silent, (3) other code is built on the decision. That puts the merge
rule first and the backfill last, the opposite of the data's flow.

| | Subproblem | Why here | Demo |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **S1** | decide a field's current value, keep what it displaced | all three: a wrong merge loses a real edit, silently | **yes** |
| **S2** | stop a change going round forever | the only self-amplifying failure: a loop eats the cap | **yes** |
| **S3** | hold outbound work on disk and spend the cap | S1's severity, lower likelihood; a known shape | **yes** |
| **S4** | make inbound delivery safe to repeat and reorder | "older" needs S1's key; severe but detectable | **yes** |
| **S5** | know which record is which across the systems | a lost create can duplicate a record: bounded, visible | no |
| **S6** | recover what was missed while a side was dark | **first to ask about**, sixth to build; rests on A4 | no |
| **S7** | prove the webhook came from Salesforce | a gate, not a risk; stubbed day one | no |
| **S8** | load the 5 million existing records | one-off, offline, no latency target | no |

**The demo exercises S1–S4 and nothing below** — the four whose failures are
unrecoverable or silent. S2, S6, S7 and S8 add **no process** of their own.

## 4. The data we store

Eight tables; Appendix C.2 has the DDL.
[ADR 0002](adr/0002-merge-per-field-not-per-record.md): **the unit of sync is a
field**, forced by the brief's own scenario — a record-level comparison would
have to discard one of two concurrent edits to different fields.

| Table | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `customer`, `contact` | **the current values**, typed; they live here and nowhere else |
| `field_version` | the **order key** per `(record, field)`, plus `sf_value` / `sf_observed_at`: a cache, not a second truth |
| `field_change` | **the history**: append-only, `applied` and `superseded`, both **permanent** |
| `sync_observation` | `echo`, `confirmed`, `restatement`; 90-day partitions; not edits by people, so not history |
| `inbound_event` | the duplicate key, 30-day retention (104 MB) — 8.1 |
| `outbound_change` | the **durable queue**: which field is owed, **never the value** — 6.3 |
| `record_link` | Salesforce id ↔ portal id, and the per-record lock |
| `echo_fence`, `sync_watermark` | "we just wrote this" (15-min TTL); how far through history we are sure |

`sf_value` is moved by a Salesforce observation **and by our own successful send**.
**Storage:** 5 M typed rows at 1.2 GB; **27 M** `field_version` rows (1 M × 3
fields + 4 M × 6) at 5.5 GB with its index; `field_change` at **26 M rows/year**
(20 M edits × 1.3 fields) and **5.2 GB/yr, kept forever because it is the
product**. **~13 GB in year one, growing 5 GB/yr.**

## 5. The inbound path

**One HTTP request becomes one Postgres transaction**, with no network call
inside it and no background step. Appendix C.3 has the sequence: validate, claim
the `eventId`, lock the record, then four steps per field, then commit and 200.

- **(a) learn** records what Salesforce holds regardless of what (c) decides,
  which is what collapses repair into the single condition 8.3.
- **(b) restatement** skips a field restating the `sf_value` we already held (8.4).
- **(c) decide** takes the first case that applies — echo, value-already-equal
  (`confirmed`), the order-key comparison, `superseded` — and only here can a
  current value change.
- **(d) repair** is condition 8.3, after every field whatever happened to it.

**The duplicate claim and the apply share one transaction:** split them and a
crash between marks an event processed that was never applied, which Salesforce
will never resend. **Fields are independent**, so one event may apply `phone` and
supersede `city`, making the event's outcome `partial`.

> A change whose canonical value already equals the current value changes
> **nothing** — not the value, not the order key, and not history.

| Resolving the record | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| **(a)** known `sf_id` | one indexed lookup, lock, proceed |
| **(b)** unknown `sf_id`, human `changedBy` | mint a `portal_id`, insert link and empty row, apply every field as a first write. **Recovery (10.3) reuses this** |
| **(c)** unknown `sf_id`, integration user | the echo of a create *we* made. **503 + `Retry-After: 5`, apply nothing**; by redelivery it is case (a). After 60 s, log loudly and treat as (b) |

**400 versus 500**, since a 400 discards the event forever: an unknown *field
name* earns one; a *value* we failed to canonicalise is our bug and earns a 500.

## 6. The outbound path

**6.1 The portal save.** The handler takes part 5's record lock, stamps
`occurred_at` from `clock_timestamp()` and the actor from the session (A9), calls
`applyChanges`, and commits — **the value change and the queue row are the same
commit**, created by **condition 8.3, as on the inbound path**.

**6.2 The worker loop** (Appendix C.4). Each tick: hold the leader lease (else
idle as a standby, [ADR 0003](adr/0003-one-sender-with-a-leader-lease.md));
reclaim rows whose 30-second lease expired; probe instead of claiming if the
breaker is open; claim **whole records**, oldest-due first so nothing starves;
read current values and build one call per record; take a governor token; send
and settle. `attempts` rises when a row is **claimed**, not when it fails, so a
row that crashes us mid-send cannot be retried forever.

**6.3 Coalescing, and reading the value late.** All fields owed on one record
become **one** call — a four-field form save is four rows and one PATCH.

> The sender reads each field's **current value at send time**, never a value
> carried on the queue row, which is why part 4 stores none.

A city edit at 09:00 and another at 11:00 during an outage therefore send **the
11:00 value, once.** On a `2xx`, **after** the response and never before, the
sender sets `sf_value` to what it sent, writes the `echo_fence` rows, and records
`sent_at` (Appendix B traces the divergence that first step prevents).

**6.4 The cap, slowing down, and the breaker. 70 of the 100 req/s,** both bounds
chosen. *Not 100:* the cap counts our retries and belongs to the client's org, so
another integration's burst would reach us as rejections, while at 70 a 30% burst
is absorbed. *Not lower:* catch-up scales inversely — 10.4 row 1 drains in
6.3 min, row 5 at a governor of 25 takes 16.0. Steady state spends ~7.4 req/s, so
we run at **11% utilisation** and the other 89% drains backlogs.

On a slow-down signal (A8), nothing is dropped:

```
rate := max(5, rate / 2)                   -- multiplicative decrease
row.state := 'pending'
row.next_attempt_at := now + (Retry-After, else 2^attempts s jittered, cap 300 s)
row.attempts := attempts - 1               -- given back: not the row's fault
recover: rate := min(70, rate + 5) per 30 s of clean responses
```

**The breaker splits two failures, and that split is what makes a 6-hour outage
survivable.** An **endpoint failure** (refused, timeout, 5xx) says nothing about
the row: after 5 consecutive ones we stop claiming and probe every 30 s, and
claimed rows return to `pending` **with attempts restored**. A **row failure**, a
400-class rejection naming this record's data, is the only kind counting attempts
toward giving up (F.6).

**6.5 Restart, and settling a group.** A restart is a non-event: the new process
takes the lease, reclaims expired rows, and resumes; a row that reached
Salesforce before the crash is sent again, safely, because all three calls are
idempotent (C.1).

| Outcome | State | Attempts | Then |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `2xx` | `sent` | — | set `sf_value`/`sf_observed_at`; write `echo_fence`; record `sent_at` |
| `429` / limit | `pending` | restored | halve the rate; honour `Retry-After` |
| timeout / refused / `5xx` | `pending` | restored | counts toward the breaker; backoff with jitter |
| `400`-class, data rejected | `failed` | kept | **alert** — a value we accept and Salesforce refuses needs a human |
| `404`, record gone | `failed` | kept | **alert** — deletes are out of scope (A15) |
| `401` / `403` | `pending` | restored | **page, stop the sender** — else the queue burns into `failed` |

A `failed` row is never deleted; it keeps its `last_error`.

## 7. The rule when both sides change the same record

**7.1 Who is doing the merging.** **Salesforce has no merge logic**, so our
database holds the decision — and hence the rule that is easy to miss: **a
webhook we reject is not a no-op.** It is the discovery that Salesforce holds a
value we rejected, and it owes an outbound call (8.3).

**7.2 The order key — the field that decides which edit is current.**

| Component | On a webhook | On a portal save |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `occurred_at` | **the payload's `occurredAt`** | **`clock_timestamp()` of the saving transaction** (A9) |
| `origin_rank` | `1` | `0` |
| `origin_event_id` | **the payload's `eventId`** | the portal change id, a ULID per save |

> **Apply the incoming change if and only if its order key is strictly greater
> than the stored one.**

`clock_timestamp()`, not `now()`, which returns the transaction's start. On an
exact tie **Salesforce wins**, the cheaper direction; a shared millisecond (A11)
breaks on `origin_event_id`, arbitrarily but **stably**. Strictness is
load-bearing: `>` and not `>=` makes re-applying an applied change a no-op (F.7).

**7.3 Canonical form.** Canonicalised **before** being compared or stored; the
stored form is canonical.

| Field | Canonical form |
| --- | --- |
| all text | Unicode NFC; trim; collapse internal whitespace runs to one space |
| `email` | the above, then lowercased whole |
| `phone` | E.164 by the contact's country; on a parse failure, digits with a leading `+`, and count it |
| `status` | mapped through the agreed picklist vocabulary |
| `customer_id` | the `portal_id` UUID, lowercase hex |
| empty | `''` and `NULL` are one thing, stored `NULL` |

Not hygiene — this is what makes part 9 true: **one formatting difference reads as
a change and turns the sync into a generator of its own traffic** (F.7).

**7.4 Different fields — the brief's own scenario.** No conflict rule needed,
which is the argument for ADR 0002: finance sets `city`, then sales changes
`phone` and the webhook names `phone` only (A3), so `city` is never looked at.
The portal ends with the new phone **and** the finance city, each with its own
actor and time (Appendix A).

**7.5 The same field. Across the two sides:** the order key decides; the winner
gets an `applied` row; **the loser is kept** as `superseded` with its value, actor
and time (the brief is explicit that an earlier edit stays on record); and **if
the loser was Salesforce's value, a repair write is enqueued** (8.3). **Two
portal users:** the record lock serialises the saves rather than tying them, so
the second wins on a later `clock_timestamp()` and the first's value survives in
`field_change` under their name. What they *see* is a product decision (open
question 4); my rule is that the portal renders each field as "set by X at T" and
names who replaced a submitted value — **no blocking, no merge dialog.**

**7.6 Two clocks: the rule for the skew window.** 7.2 compares Salesforce's clock
against ours, so inside the skew window (A10: 2 s) an edit made second can rank
first.

> **The order key stays authoritative inside the window; we do not detect or
> correct an inversion. We bound the skew, and we measure and page on the
> inversions.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Bound** | hosts run NTP; drift above **500 ms** is a host alarm, so at most a quarter of A10's 2 s is ours |
| **Measure** | **cross-side near-tie inversions/hour**: `superseded` rows whose superseding change has the opposite `origin` and `abs(Δ occurred_at) ≤ 2 s` |
| **Warn / page** | 5/hour; **20/hour**, or a rolling 4-hour window where **≥ 80%** of inversions favour one origin |

The bias threshold does the work: genuine races go both ways, so a sustained
one-directional result is the signature of real skew. **No deterministic in-window
tiebreak is offered** (F.7).

## 8. Duplicates and out-of-order changes

**8.1 A duplicate webhook. `eventId` is the idempotency key, claimed in the same
transaction as the apply.** No row from the `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` means we have
seen it: commit, answer `200 {"status":"duplicate"}`, change nothing. Salesforce
has done nothing wrong (A7), so this is counted, not alerted. Two independent
layers, **and only the second is the guarantee:** *suppression*, the table, so a
duplicate does no work; and *harmlessness*, the strict `>` of 7.2, which makes an
unsuppressed duplicate a no-op anyway — the table falls to a prune or a truncate,
the compare holds regardless (F.8). A repeated `eventId` carrying a *different*
`payload_hash` is a provider bug: first write wins, and this one **is** alerted.

**8.2 An older webhook after a newer one.**

> **Compare order keys per field; a change not strictly newer never becomes
> current, and is recorded `superseded`.**

```
evt_A  phone -> ...0001  occurredAt 11:30:04.000    evt_B  phone -> ...0002  11:30:09.000

B first:  11:30:09 > stored           -> APPLIED. current ...0002,
                                         sf_value ...0002, sf_observed_at 11:30:09
A second: (a) 11:30:04 NOT > 11:30:09 -> sf_value LEFT ALONE (a later SF state is known)
          (c) 11:30:04 < 11:30:09     -> SUPERSEDED. history keeps ...0001,
                                         sales.user, 11:30:04; current stays ...0002
          (d) sf_value = current      -> NO repair write
```

Step (a) is what makes this correct rather than merely plausible: `evt_A`
describes a **past** state of Salesforce, so `sf_value` must not move. **No
reordering buffer** — A11 gives no sequence numbers, so we cannot detect that
anything is *missing* (F.8).

**8.3 The repair write — one condition for every case.**

> **After every field, regardless of what happened to it: if
> `field_version.sf_value` is distinct from the current value, enqueue a repair
> write.**

"Distinct from" is SQL's `IS DISTINCT FROM`, and the NULL case is load-bearing:
**an `sf_value` we have never learned is distinct from any current value.**
Without it every portal-created record would be stranded.

| What happened | `sf_value` after | Current | Repair? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Salesforce change applied | the new value | the same | no |
| Salesforce value superseded by a newer portal edit | Salesforce's | ours | **yes** |
| older event after a newer one (8.2) | unchanged | matches it | no |
| echo of our own write | what we sent | the same | no |
| Salesforce restates a value we hold | that value | the same | no |
| full-record restatement during an outage (8.4) | Salesforce's stale value | our unsent edit | **yes** |

It **terminates** — the repair sends our current value, the echo sets `sf_value`
to it, the condition goes false — and it is the **entire logic of outage
recovery** (10.3).

**8.4 If a webhook carries the full record instead.** A3 assumes
changed-fields-only, and **full-record mode is the dangerous one**, because a
field's silence and its restatement look identical. *The hazard:* finance sets
`city` to Noida at 15:00, unsent; at 16:00 a sales user changes the phone and the
full-record payload restates `city: "Gurugram"`, stamped 16:00. Compared as a
change, `16:00 > 15:00`, so we would **overwrite the finance edit with an older
value Salesforce was merely restating.**

> *The rule,* step (b) of the apply: **a field whose canonical value equals the
> `sf_value` we already held is a restatement — not restamped, not compared, not
> touched.**

Traced: `sf_value[city]` is already `Gurugram`, so `city` is skipped and stays
Noida while 8.3 enqueues the repair we already owed; `phone` differs and applies
normally. **Step (b) is unconditional**, whatever the payload shape, which is why
`applyChanges` needs no mode parameter — and the outage sweep (10.3) requires it
regardless.

## 9. The rule that stops a loop

Ranked second of eight: a loop consumes the whole 100 req/s budget and stops sync
for every record at once, within seconds of deployment.

> **9.1 — L1, the structural rule.** Outbound work is created exactly when
> `field_version.sf_value` differs from a field's current value — condition 8.3,
> after every field, on both paths, and nowhere else.

```
portal sets city = Noida  -> sf_value "Gurugram" <> "Noida"  -> 1 outbound row
we PATCH Noida, 2xx       -> sf_value := "Noida"                            (6.3)
Salesforce echoes Noida   -> sf_value "Noida" = current       -> 0 rows.  Dead.
```

No fuel after one hop, because there is nothing left to disagree about.
**Precondition: canonical form (7.3).**

> **9.2 — L2, the actor rule.** A webhook whose `changedBy` is the integration user
> (A6) is an echo: recorded, never compared, never applied.

L1 guarantees the loop stops; L2 that it stops on the **right value**, since an
echo carries a later time than the edit our write overwrote and would otherwise
launder a stale value over a newer one (Appendix B).

> **9.3 — L3, the echo fence.** After a 2xx the sender records the record, field and
> hash of the canonical value sent, expiring in 15 minutes; an inbound change
> matching an unexpired entry is an echo.

> **9.4 — L4, the repair breaker.** Above **5 repairs to one field in an hour**,
> enqueue nothing more for it, mark it contested, and alert.

L3 is L2's guarantee keyed on the value rather than the actor, so it holds if A6
is false. L4 bounds the one way L1 fails: a spelling our canonical form does not
normalise makes every echo read as disagreement.

| | Guarantees | Absent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **L1** + canonical form | the loop **terminates** | everything; no other layer saves us |
| **L2** | it terminates on the **right value** | our own write launders a stale value over a newer one |
| L3 | L2's guarantee without A6 | nothing, while A6 holds |
| L4 | bounds L1's one failure mode | an unbounded argument over one field |

## 10. The 6-hour outage

**10.1 What it is.** Six hours with the Salesforce API unreachable and webhooks
sent during it possibly never arriving — dark both ways at once (A16).

**The arithmetic uses the business-hours average of 3 edits/s, not A1's 20/s
peak.** Saying so up front because the two differ greatly — about 6 minutes
against about 35 — and the choice is a judgement, not an oversight: a peak is a
15-minute phenomenon, and six consecutive hours of one is not credible. The peak
is carried as row 3 of 10.4, so both numbers are on the page. **The portal keeps
working throughout:** edits apply locally and queue for Salesforce, so the only
cost is visibility there, and the 30-second target does not apply during catch-up.

**10.2 What is on disk.**

| | At the worst moment | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `outbound_change`, `pending` | **19,440 rows, ~4.9 MB** | each committed with the edit that caused it (6.1) |
| rows left `inflight` by a restart | a handful | reclaimed when the 30-second lease expires |
| `sync_watermark` | one row per object type | where the sweep resumes |

Five megabytes is what "pending calls must still be there after our process
restarts" costs, and **a restart during the outage is a non-event.**

**10.3 How we drain it — and why the order is not negotiable.**

> **The inbound sweep must complete before the outbound drain begins.**

The loss it prevents: finance sets a city to Noida at 15:00, queued unsent; at
17:00 a sales user sets it to Delhi in Salesforce and that webhook never arrives.
*Drain first:* we PATCH Noida, Delhi is overwritten, and the sweep reads back our
own value — **Delhi is destroyed with no record it existed.** *Sweep first:*
Delhi's 17:00 `SystemModstamp` beats the portal's 15:00, Noida is kept as
`superseded` under the finance user's name, and the queued row then sends the
**current** value (6.3) — Delhi, a no-op.

With 14,954 portal-touched and 34,892 Salesforce-touched records out of 5 M
(row 1), the expected overlap is `14,954 × 34,892 / 5,000,000` = **104 records**,
and the ordering costs no time. **The sweep also depends on the restatement rule
(8.4)**, since a `SystemModstamp` is a *record's* time, so a record touched at
17:00 hands back every field stamped 17:00. Appendix C.5 has the sequence: probe,
hold the drain, page through the changed-since query feeding each record in as a
full-record observation, advance the watermark per page, release at half rate.

**10.4 The arithmetic — every figure, in one table.** Every number in this
document comes out of these lines; the table varies one assumption per row.

```
window           6 h x 3600                                 = 21,600 s
queued changes   portal edits/s x 21,600
outbound calls   queued changes / 1.3 changes per record      (coalescing, 6.3)
drain capacity   governor - 7.4 req/s reserved for live traffic
                 (7.4 = peak steady state: (6 + 0.7 repairs) x 1.1 retries, 6.4)
drain            resume at half the governor, +5 req/s every 30 s, then full
sweep            Salesforce records / 2,000 per SOQL page     (requests)
                 Salesforce records / 500 per second          (local apply)
total            sweep + drain  -- the sweep blocks the drain (10.3)
```

| # | Scenario | What varies | portal /s | queued | calls | drain | SF records | reqs | sweep | **total** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **base** | — | 0.90 | 19,440 | 14,954 | 5.1 | 34,892 | 18 | 1.2 | **6.3** |
| 2 | no coalescing | 1.0 chg/rec | 0.90 | 19,440 | 19,440 | 6.3 | 34,892 | 18 | 1.2 | **7.5** |
| 3 | sustained peak | A1 → 20/s | 6.00 | 129,600 | 99,692 | 27.7 | 232,615 | 117 | 7.8 | **35.4** |
| 4 | portal-heavy | A2 → 70% portal | 2.10 | 45,360 | 34,892 | 12.0 | 14,954 | 8 | 0.5 | **12.5** |
| 5 | contended cap | A12 → governor 25 | 0.90 | 19,440 | 14,954 | 14.8 | 34,892 | 18 | 1.2 | **16.0** |
| 6 | no changed-since | A4 false → all 5 M | 0.90 | 19,440 | 14,954 | 5.1 | 5,000,000 | 2,500 | 16.7 | **21.8** |

Drain, sweep and total are minutes. **Row 1 is the answer: about 6 minutes.**

```
Row 1, with the division shown
queued     0.9 x 21,600                             = 19,440 changes
calls      19,440 / 1.3                             = 14,954
capacity   70 - 7.4                                 = 62.6 req/s at full rate
ramp       35,40,45,50,55,60,65 req/s, 30 s each, each minus 7.4:
           (27.6+32.6+37.6+42.6+47.6+52.6+57.6) x 30 = 8,946 calls in 210 s
rest       (14,954 - 8,946) / 62.6                  = 96.0 s
drain      210 + 96.0 = 306.0 s                     = 5.1 minutes
sweep      2.1 x 21,600 / 1.3                       = 34,892 records
           34,892 / 2,000 = 18 requests (0.3 s of budget)
           34,892 / 500   = 69.8 s                  = 1.2 minutes
TOTAL      1.2 + 5.1                                = 6.3 minutes
```

Allow **under 10 minutes** operationally, covering page-fetch latency, retries,
and the breaker needing a few probes to close. **Beyond row 1:** the **cap is the
floor, not our design** — row 3 at the full 100 req/s with no reserve is still
`99,692 / 100 = 997 s = 16.6 min`, so our 30% reserve costs ~11 minutes in the
worst credible case (A12). **Row 6 demotes A4** from load-bearing to preferable,
and I would run that sweep **nightly regardless**, as the standing net under lost
webhooks, canonicalisation gaps, fields L4 gave up on, and 7.6's inversions.

## 11. Three numbers I would watch

One per failure mode: outbound stuck, inbound slow, and getting it wrong. The
third is the only one that detects incorrectness rather than slowness.

| | Number | Normal | Warn | **Call someone** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **age of the oldest unsent change** — `min(created_at)` over `pending` | < 5 s | 60 s | **300 s (5 min)** |
| **2** | **inbound lag** — p99 `applied_at − occurred_at`, Salesforce-origin, last 5 min | < 6 s | 20 s | **> 30 s for 5 min** |
| **3** | **divergence** — repairs + Salesforce-origin `superseded` per minute; **and** 7.6's inversions per hour | ~0; < 1/h | 10/min; 5/h | **100/min; 20/h; or ≥ 80% one-way over 4 h** |

**Age, not depth,** for number 1: 19,000 rows draining fast is healthy, 3 rows
stuck is not. Number 2 **includes Salesforce's own emission delay**, because the
30 seconds we promised is end to end. Number 3 is the only one that reports a skew
past A10, a canonicalisation gap, or a loop rule that stopped working. **On the
dashboard but not paging:** the governor's rate and 429 count, the breaker's
state, rows in `failed` and fields marked contested, signature failures and 400s,
and `sync_watermark` lag.

## 12. What I am leaving out

**Because the exercise says so:** deletes (A15), Salesforce login screens, any
visual UI, a second region, and load testing real Salesforce. Where code exists
it runs against a fake Salesforce I wrote.

**Because I chose to:** the **initial 5 M backfill** (S8, costed as row 6 of
10.4); **Salesforce auth lifecycle** (mechanical); **schema-change handling** (L4
degrades an unknown picklist value into a contested field, not a loop);
**merging already-duplicated records** (a pre-existing data-quality problem);
**field-level permissions** (open question 6); **objects and fields beyond the
nine** (A14); **the portal's overwrite notice** (7.5's rule is designed, the UI
is not); **right-to-erasure against permanent history** (open question 5); and
**the monitoring plumbing** (part 11 has the queries).

**What I would build first:** S1 and S2 alone for a week — the merge rule, the
history, canonical form, and the one condition — against a fake Salesforce;
everything after is plumbing around a decision that has to be right first. And I
would get open question 1 answered first: Change Data Capture replay ids would
retire A11, strengthen 8.2 from ordering-what-arrived to detecting-what-is-missing,
and turn the recovery sweep into a replay.

1	/**
2	 * The merge: what one edit does to one record's fields (design 5, 7, 8).
3	 *
4	 * This is the module the exercise is about. Everything else moves data to and
5	 * from it.
6	 *
7	 * **The shape is the design's and must not be rearranged.** Per field, in this
8	 * order: **learn**, then **restatement**, then **decide**, then **repair**.
9	 *
10	 * - **(a) learn** records what Salesforce holds *before* anything is decided
11	 *   and *regardless* of what is decided. A webhook we reject is not a no-op:
12	 *   it is the discovery that Salesforce holds a value we rejected, and since
13	 *   Salesforce has no merge logic (design 7.1) nobody else will fix that. This
14	 *   separation is what collapses the whole repair rule into the single
15	 *   condition of step (d).
16	 * - **(b) restatement** skips a field whose value equals the `sf_value` we
17	 *   already held, because a full-record payload restates unchanged fields with
18	 *   a fresh record-level timestamp (design 8.4).
19	 * - **(c) decide** takes the first case that applies — echo, then a value
20	 *   equal to the one we already hold, then the order-key comparison — and only
21	 *   here can a current value change.
22	 * - **(d) repair** is one condition, checked after every field whatever
23	 *   happened to it: if we believe Salesforce disagrees with us, we owe
24	 *   Salesforce a call (design 8.3, 9.1).
25	 *
26	 * What a caller must know:
27	 *
28	 * - **The caller owns the transaction.** `applyChanges` never begins or commits
29	 *   one. The design requires the duplicate claim and the apply to share a
30	 *   transaction (design 5, 8.1): split across two commits, a crash in between
31	 *   marks an event processed that was never applied, and Salesforce will never
32	 *   resend it.
33	 * - **The caller has already resolved the record link** and created the record
34	 *   row (design 5's cases (a) and (b)). Called for a record that does not
35	 *   exist, the store raises `StoreReadError`, which is deliberately allowed to
36	 *   propagate: it means a bug in the caller, not bad input, and the
37	 *   transaction must roll back rather than half-apply.
38	 * - **Fields are independent.** One event may apply `phone` and supersede
39	 *   `city`; the event's own outcome is then `partial` (design 5), which the
40	 *   caller derives from the returned rows.
41	 * - **An unknown field name raises `WebhookRejected` (400).** Validation should
42	 *   have caught it first; this is the backstop, and it aborts the whole event
43	 *   rather than applying some fields and rejecting others, because the caller's
44	 *   transaction is what makes that all-or-nothing.
45	 * - **No network call happens here**, which is what keeps the inbound
46	 *   endpoint's p99 at 200 ms and stops a Salesforce outage becoming held
47	 *   database locks (design 5).
48	 */
49	
50	import { canonicalise } from "./canonical.js";
51	import { sortFields } from "./fields.js";
52	import { isStrictlyNewer, makeOrderKey } from "./orderKey.js";
53	import type {
54	  AppliedField,
55	  ApplyChangesInput,
56	  FieldOutcome,
57	  OrderKey,
58	  OutboundReason,
59	} from "./types.js";
60	import type { FieldVersionRow } from "../store/schema.js";
61	import type { Tx } from "../store/store.js";
62	
63	/**
64	 * Apply one edit's changes to one record, and return what happened to each
65	 * field.
66	 *
67	 * @param tx an open transaction, owned by the caller.
68	 * @param input one edit — see {@link ApplyChangesInput}.
69	 * @returns one {@link AppliedField} per field in `rawChanges`, in catalogue
70	 *   order.
71	 * @throws {WebhookRejected} 400, when a field name is not in the catalogue.
72	 * @throws {StoreReadError} when the record was not resolved before the call.
73	 */
74	export function applyChanges(tx: Tx, input: ApplyChangesInput): AppliedField[] {
75	  // Fixed order, so two runs over the same payload produce identical history.
76	  // (The record-level lock is what serialises competing merges; this only
77	  // makes the output deterministic.)
78	  const fields = sortFields(input.objectType, Object.keys(input.rawChanges));
79	
80	  const applied: AppliedField[] = [];
81	  for (const field of fields) {
82	    applied.push(applyOneField(tx, input, field));
83	  }
84	  return applied;
85	}
86	
87	/**
88	 * One field through the four steps. Separate from the loop so the four steps
89	 * read in order and nothing can accidentally be hoisted between fields.
90	 */
91	function applyOneField(
92	  tx: Tx,
93	  input: ApplyChangesInput,
94	  field: string,
95	): AppliedField {
96	  const { objectType, portalId } = input;
97	
98	  // `field` came from Object.keys(rawChanges), so the entry exists; the `??`
99	  // satisfies noUncheckedIndexedAccess and never hides a missing field.
100	  const raw = input.rawChanges[field] ?? null;
101	
102	  // Canonical **before** comparing or storing (design 7.3). Without this, one
103	  // formatting difference between the two systems reads as a change and the
104	  // sync becomes a generator of its own traffic (design 9.1).
105	  const value = canonicalise(objectType, field, raw);
106	
107	  const versionBefore = tx.getFieldVersion(objectType, portalId, field);
108	  const currentBefore = currentValueOf(tx, input, field);
109	
110	  // ---------------------------------------------------------------- (a) learn
111	  //
112	  // Unconditional, before anything is decided. An event we reject still
113	  // teaches us Salesforce's state, and that is what lets step (d) be one
114	  // condition instead of a case analysis (design 5, 8.3).
115	  //
116	  // The snapshot is taken here, before step (a) moves anything, because step
117	  // (b) must compare against the `sf_value` we held *before* this event.
118	  const sfValueHeldBefore = versionBefore?.sfValue;
119	  let sfValue = versionBefore?.sfValue;
120	  let sfObservedAtMs = versionBefore?.sfObservedAtMs;
121	
122	  if (input.origin === "salesforce") {
123	    if (sfObservedAtMs === undefined || input.occurredAtMs > sfObservedAtMs) {
124	      sfValue = value;
125	      sfObservedAtMs = input.occurredAtMs;
126	    }
127	    // else: leave `sfValue` alone — we already know a LATER Salesforce state.
128	    //
129	    // This guard is why design 8.2 is correct and not merely plausible.
130	    // Without it, an out-of-order event would set `sf_value` to a *past*
131	    // Salesforce value, condition (d) would read a disagreement that does not
132	    // exist, and we would spend a repair call arguing with Salesforce about a
133	    // value it no longer holds.
134	  }
135	  // A portal edit teaches us nothing about Salesforce: only a Salesforce
136	  // observation, or our own successful send (design 6.3, outside this module),
137	  // may move `sf_value`.
138	
139	  // --------------------------------------------------------- (b) restatement
140	  //
141	  // A field whose canonical value equals the `sf_value` we already held is
142	  // Salesforce *restating* a value, not changing it — so step (c) is skipped
143	  // entirely: not restamped, not compared, not touched (design 8.4).
144	  //
145	  // Why this is not an optimisation. A `SystemModstamp` is a **record's**
146	  // modification time, not a field's, so a full-record payload restates every
147	  // unchanged field with a fresh timestamp. Compared as changes, those
148	  // restatements would beat a portal edit made during an outage and overwrite
149	  // it with Salesforce's stale value — exactly the data loss this design
150	  // exists to prevent (design 8.4, 10.3).
151	  //
152	  // Two conditions beyond the value match:
153	  //
154	  // - Only for `origin === "salesforce"`. A portal user typing back the value
155	  //   Salesforce holds is a real edit by a real person with a real order key.
156	  // - Only when `sfValueHeldBefore` is defined. An absent `sf_value` (the
157	  //   design's SQL NULL) means we have never heard Salesforce's value for this
158	  //   field, so the incoming value is a change, not a restatement.
159	  const isRestatement =
160	    input.origin === "salesforce" &&
161	    sfValueHeldBefore !== undefined &&
162	    value === sfValueHeldBefore;
163	
164	  // -------------------------------------------------------------- (c) decide
165	  let outcome: FieldOutcome;
166	  let newKey: OrderKey | undefined;
167	
168	  const incoming = makeOrderKey(input.occurredAtMs, input.origin, input.originEventId);
169	  const stored = storedKeyOf(versionBefore);
170	
171	  if (isRestatement) {
172	    // Step (c) is skipped. Step (d) still runs — the field may well be a
173	    // disagreement we owe Salesforce a call about, and in the outage trace of
174	    // design 8.4 it is precisely the repair we already owed.
175	    outcome = "restatement";
176	    tx.appendObservation({
177	      objectType,
178	      portalId,
179	      field,
180	      observedValue: value,
181	      occurredAtMs: input.occurredAtMs,
182	      origin: input.origin,
183	      originEventId: input.originEventId,
184	      actor: input.actor,
185	      outcome: "restatement",
186	    });
187	  } else if (input.isEcho === true) {
188	    // L2, the actor rule (design 9.2): a webhook describing a write of ours is
189	    // recorded, never compared, never applied.
190	    //
191	    // Load-bearing, not an economy measure. L1 guarantees the loop stops; L2
192	    // guarantees it stops on the *right value*. The echo of our own write
193	    // carries the time Salesforce stored it, which is later than the edit that
194	    // write overwrote — so compared as a change it would win, and it would
195	    // launder our value back over a newer edit from the other side. Appendix B
196	    // traces exactly that overwrite race.
197	    //
198	    // Note what is *not* consulted here: the value. "Never applied" must hold
199	    // whatever the echo carries, or the guarantee would depend on Salesforce
200	    // echoing precisely what we sent.
201	    outcome = "echo";
202	    tx.appendObservation({
203	      objectType,
204	      portalId,
205	      field,
206	      observedValue: value,
207	      occurredAtMs: input.occurredAtMs,
208	      origin: input.origin,
209	      originEventId: input.originEventId,
210	      actor: input.actor,
211	      outcome: "echo",
212	    });
213	  } else if (value === currentBefore) {
214	    // A change whose canonical value already equals the current value changes
215	    // nothing — not the value, not the order key, and not history. Checked
216	    // **before** the order-key comparison, for two reasons:
217	    //
218	    // 1. `field_change` is the client's record of edits that *changed*
219	    //    something. A re-save of the value already held is not one, and
220	    //    filling permanent history with no-op rows would make "who changed the
221	    //    city" harder to answer — which is the thing the client is actually
222	    //    buying (design 4, and the brief's own ask).
223	    // 2. It must not restamp the order key. If a no-op re-save advanced the
224	    //    stamp, it would take ownership of the field from a genuine edit: a
225	    //    later real edit from the other side could then lose to someone who
226	    //    re-submitted a value they did not change.
227	    //
228	    // This is a third layer of idempotence beneath the duplicate table and the
229	    // strict `>` of design 7.2 — and the strict `>` is still the backstop that
230	    // matters, because it is what handles a *different* value arriving with an
231	    // older stamp (design 8.1 layer 2, 8.2).
232	    outcome = "confirmed";
233	    tx.appendObservation({
234	      objectType,
235	      portalId,
236	      field,
237	      observedValue: value,
238	      occurredAtMs: input.occurredAtMs,
239	      origin: input.origin,
240	      originEventId: input.originEventId,
241	      actor: input.actor,
242	      outcome: "confirmed",
243	    });
244	  } else if (stored === undefined || isStrictlyNewer(incoming, stored)) {
245	    // Strictly greater, `>` and not `>=` (design 7.2): re-applying a change
246	    // already applied does nothing, so the inbound path is idempotent
247	    // independently of the duplicate table (design 8.1 layer 2). No stored key
248	    // at all means nothing has ever won this field, so this change wins.
249	    outcome = "applied";
250	    newKey = incoming;
251	    tx.setCurrentValue(objectType, portalId, field, value);
252	    tx.appendFieldChange({
253	      objectType,
254	      portalId,
255	      field,
256	      oldValue: currentBefore,
257	      newValue: value,
258	      occurredAtMs: input.occurredAtMs,
259	      origin: input.origin,
260	      originEventId: input.originEventId,
261	      actor: input.actor,
262	      outcome: "applied",
263	    });
264	  } else {
265	    // A real edit by a real person, to a value we do not hold, that lost the
266	    // order-key comparison. Kept with its value, actor and time, because the
267	    // brief is explicit that the fact of an earlier edit stays on record
268	    // (design 7.5).
269	    //
270	    // No `value !== currentBefore` guard is needed here: the equality branch
271	    // above has already taken every change that matches what we hold, so
272	    // everything reaching this branch is a genuine disagreement about the
273	    // value — which is also why a `superseded` row always records a real
274	    // difference rather than a no-op.
275	    outcome = "superseded";
276	    tx.appendFieldChange({
277	      objectType,
278	      portalId,
279	      field,
280	      oldValue: currentBefore,
281	      newValue: value,
282	      occurredAtMs: input.occurredAtMs,
283	      origin: input.origin,
284	      originEventId: input.originEventId,
285	      actor: input.actor,
286	      outcome: "superseded",
287	    });
288	  }
289	
290	  // Persist the order key together with what step (a) learned. One write,
291	  // whatever happened above: when (c) did not apply the change, the existing
292	  // order key is kept and only the Salesforce columns move — otherwise what we
293	  // learned in (a) would be lost the moment the event lost the comparison, and
294	  // step (d) would have nothing to compare on the next event.
295	  writeFieldVersion(tx, input, field, { versionBefore, newKey, sfValue, sfObservedAtMs });
296	
297	  const currentAfter = currentValueOf(tx, input, field);
298	
299	  // -------------------------------------------------------------- (d) repair
300	  //
301	  // **One condition, after every field, whatever happened to it** (design 8.3):
302	  // if `field_version.sf_value` is distinct from our current value — including
303	  // when we have never heard it — we owe Salesforce a call.
304	  //
305	  // Why one condition is enough. Salesforce has no merge logic (design 7.1),
306	  // so we are the only party that compares anything and its copy is a
307	  // projection of our decision. The six cases of design 8.3's table — applied,
308	  // superseded, out-of-order, echo, confirmed, restatement — differ only in
309	  // what `sf_value` and the current value *are* by the time we get here, which
310	  // is what step (a) and step (c) have just settled. There is no case analysis
311	  // left to do.
312	  //
313	  // It terminates: the repair sends our current value, the echo of that write
314	  // sets `sf_value` equal to it, and the condition goes false (design 9.1).
315	  // Canonical form (design 7.3) is the precondition — two spellings of one
316	  // value are the only way to give the loop fuel.
317	  const enqueuedOutbound = enqueueRepairIfNeeded(tx, input, field, {
318	    sfValue,
319	    currentAfter,
320	  });
321	
322	  return {
323	    field,

331	/**
332	 * Step (d): enqueue the outbound call this field owes, if it owes one.
333	 *
334	 * @returns whether a row was added. False means either that we believe
335	 *   Salesforce agrees with us, that a call for this field is already pending,
336	 *   or that the breaker of design 9.4 has tripped.
337	 */
338	function enqueueRepairIfNeeded(
339	  tx: Tx,
340	  input: ApplyChangesInput,
341	  field: string,
342	  args: { sfValue: string | null | undefined; currentAfter: string | null },
343	): boolean {
344	  const { sfValue, currentAfter } = args;
345	
346	  // "**Is distinct from**", in SQL's exact sense (design 8.3, and the SQL in
347	  // Appendix C.2): an `sf_value` we have never learned IS distinct from any
348	  // current value, because "we do not know what Salesforce holds" is itself a
349	  // disagreement we owe a call about.
350	  //
351	  // Without this, a portal edit to a field Salesforce has never mentioned
352	  // would enqueue nothing and Salesforce would never learn the value at all —
353	  // every portal-created record would be stranded, which is the opposite of
354	  // what the restart and outage paths require (design 6.5, 10.3).
355	  //
356	  // It opens no hole in the cases that must stay silent, because step (a) sets
357	  // `sfValue` for every Salesforce-origin field before (d) runs: an applied
358	  // change, an echo, a confirmation and an out-of-order event all arrive here
359	  // with `sfValue` already equal to the current value.
360	  const sfKnown = sfValue !== undefined;
361	  const owed = !sfKnown || sfValue !== currentAfter;
362	  if (!owed) return false;
363	
364	  const { objectType, portalId } = input;
365	
366	  // Rule L4, the repair breaker, checked **first** (design 9.4).
367	  //
368	  // It bounds the one way L1 fails: a value Salesforce stores in a spelling
369	  // our canonical form does not normalise makes every echo read as
370	  // disagreement, and the two systems then argue at one request per round trip
371	  // forever — spending the whole 100 req/s budget and stopping sync for every
372	  // record at once. Above 5 repairs to one field in an hour we keep serving our
373	  // value and stop arguing: knowingly different on one field beats spending
374	  // the cap on an argument neither side can win.
375	  if (tx.repairsInLastHour(objectType, portalId, field) > 5) {
376	    // The design marks the field contested and alerts. This demo has no
377	    // alerting surface and no column for it, so the fact is emitted as a
378	    // process warning rather than dropped: a breaker that trips silently would
379	    // leave the two systems knowingly different with nobody told, which is the
380	    // one outcome worse than the argument it ended.
381	    process.emitWarning(
382	      `repair breaker tripped: ${objectType} ${portalId}.${field} is contested ` +
383	        `(we hold ${JSON.stringify(currentAfter)}, Salesforce holds ${JSON.stringify(sfValue)})`,
384	    );
385	    return false;
386	  }
387	
388	  // `portal-edit` when the edit we are publishing came from the portal,
389	  // `repair` when we are ending a disagreement we detected. The condition is
390	  // the same on both paths (design 9.1); only the reason differs, and it is
391	  // what the breaker above counts.
392	  const reason: OutboundReason = input.origin === "portal" ? "portal-edit" : "repair";
393	
394	  // False here means a pending row already exists for this field — the partial
395	  // unique index of design 4, which is what stops an echo arriving beside an
396	  // already-queued repair from piling up a second call (Appendix B step 5).
397	  // The queue holds no value, so the one row sends whatever is current at send
398	  // time (design 6.3).
399	  return tx.enqueueOutbound({
400	    objectType,
401	    portalId,
402	    field,
403	    reason,
404	    occurredAtMs: input.occurredAtMs,
405	  });
406	}

408	/** The field's committed current value, or `null` when we hold none. */
409	function currentValueOf(tx: Tx, input: ApplyChangesInput, field: string): string | null {
410	  const record = tx.getRecord(input.objectType, input.portalId);
411	  return record?.values[field] ?? null;
412	}

414	/** The order key of the change currently winning this field, if any. */

418	    occurredAtMs: version.occurredAtMs,
419	    originRank: version.originRank,
420	    originEventId: version.originEventId,

424	/**

426	 * believe Salesforce holds.

429	 * key is preserved, because the change that is winning has not changed.
430	 */
431	function writeFieldVersion(
432	  tx: Tx,
433	  input: ApplyChangesInput,
434	  field: string,
435	  args: {

437	    newKey: OrderKey | undefined;
438	    sfValue: string | null | undefined;

440	  },

442	  const { versionBefore, newKey, sfValue, sfObservedAtMs } = args;
443	
444	  const base: FieldVersionRow = versionBefore ?? {

467	          origin: input.origin,

471	    sfObservedAtMs,
