1	/**
2	 * The order key: the comparable value that decides which of two changes to one
3	 * field is current (design 7.2).
4	 *
5	 * Two changes to one field are always comparable, and the comparison gives the
6	 * same answer wherever and whenever it is made. Three components, compared
7	 * left to right:
8	 *
9	 * | Component        | On a webhook        | On a portal save                     |
10	 * | ---------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
11	 * | `occurredAtMs`   | the payload's time  | `clock_timestamp()` of the save (A9) |
12	 * | `originRank`     | salesforce = 1      | portal = 0                           |
13	 * | `originEventId`  | the `eventId`       | the portal change id (a ULID)        |
14	 *
15	 * What a caller must know:
16	 *
17	 * - **Apply an incoming change if and only if its key is _strictly_ greater
18	 *   than the stored one** — {@link isStrictlyNewer}, and nothing else.
19	 * - The comparison is **total**: no two keys are incomparable, so there is no
20	 *   case for a caller to handle.
21	 * - It is **stable**: the same two keys always compare the same way, in any
22	 *   process, on any day. Redelivery depends on this.
23	 * - It carries no notion of *correctness across clocks*. Inside the skew
24	 *   window (design 7.6, assumption A10: 2 s) an edit made second can rank
25	 *   first, and the design's deliberate answer is that the key stays
26	 *   authoritative while the inversions are measured and paged on — not that
27	 *   this module should try to detect them.
28	 */
29	
30	import type { OrderKey, Origin } from "./types.js";
31	import { ORIGIN_RANK } from "./types.js";
32	
33	/**
34	 * Build the key for one change.
35	 *
36	 * @param occurredAtMs the payload's `occurredAt`, or `clock_timestamp()` of the
37	 *   saving transaction — never a time supplied by an untrusted caller (A9).
38	 * @param origin the system the edit was made in.
39	 * @param originEventId the webhook's `eventId`, or the portal change id.
40	 */
41	export function makeOrderKey(
42	  occurredAtMs: number,
43	  origin: Origin,
44	  originEventId: string,
45	): OrderKey {
46	  return {
47	    occurredAtMs,
48	    // Taken from the shared table rather than written as a literal here: the
49	    // rank is the *rule*, and two copies of a rule are one edit away from
50	    // disagreeing.
51	    originRank: ORIGIN_RANK[origin],
52	    originEventId,
53	  };
54	}
55	
56	/**
57	 * Compare two keys: negative when `a` is older, zero when they are equal,
58	 * positive when `a` is newer.
59	 *
60	 * The return value is a sort comparator, so `[...keys].sort(compareOrderKeys)`
61	 * puts the oldest change first.
62	 */
63	export function compareOrderKeys(a: OrderKey, b: OrderKey): number {
64	  // Time first. Rank is only a tiebreak: consulted before time, it would make
65	  // Salesforce win every comparison and the portal could never hold a value.
66	  if (a.occurredAtMs !== b.occurredAtMs) {
67	    return a.occurredAtMs < b.occurredAtMs ? -1 : 1;
68	  }
69	
70	  // Then rank, so an exact-millisecond tie goes to Salesforce (rank 1 over the
71	  // portal's 0). That is the *cheaper* direction, not an arbitrary one: a
72	  // losing portal value costs nothing, while a losing Salesforce value obliges
73	  // us to send a repair write (design 7.2, 8.3). Breaking the tie the other
74	  // way would be correct and would simply buy us an extra outbound call every
75	  // time it happened.
76	  if (a.originRank !== b.originRank) {
77	    return a.originRank < b.originRank ? -1 : 1;
78	  }
79	
80	  // Last, the event id — because two Salesforce edits can share a millisecond
81	  // (assumption A11) and the comparison must still be total. Which id wins is
82	  // arbitrary; that it is **stable** is the point, because a redelivered event
83	  // must rank the same way the second time, or the "duplicate does nothing"
84	  // guarantee of design 8.1 layer 2 would depend on arrival order.
85	  //
86	  // Plain code-unit comparison, deliberately not `localeCompare`: a
87	  // locale-dependent or ICU-version-dependent collation would make the answer
88	  // differ between two processes comparing the same two keys, which is exactly
89	  // the stability this component exists to provide.
90	  if (a.originEventId === b.originEventId) return 0;
91	  return a.originEventId < b.originEventId ? -1 : 1;
92	}
93	
94	/**
95	 * Whether an incoming change may become the current value.
96	 *
97	 * **Strictly** greater, `>` and not `>=`, and that is load-bearing: it makes
98	 * re-applying a change whose key equals the stored one a no-op, so the inbound
99	 * path is idempotent *independently of the duplicate table* (design 8.1 layer
100	 * 2). The table is only suppression, and it falls to a prune, a restore or a
101	 * truncate; this comparison is the guarantee that survives all three. A design
102	 * resting on the table alone is one retention policy away from corrupting
103	 * data.
104	 */
105	export function isStrictlyNewer(incoming: OrderKey, stored: OrderKey): boolean {
106	  return compareOrderKeys(incoming, stored) > 0;
107	}

1	/**
2	 * Canonical form: the single spelling of a value that every comparison uses
3	 * (design 7.3).
4	 *
5	 * **Why this module exists at all.** It looks like hygiene and it is not: it is
6	 * what makes the loop rule of design 9.1 true. Send Salesforce
7	 * `+919876543210`, let Salesforce store `+91 98765 43210`, and the echo of our
8	 * own write comes back reading as a *different* value with a *later* time. We
9	 * would apply it, our current value would change, that change would create
10	 * outbound work, and that work would echo again. One formatting difference
11	 * turns the sync into a generator of its own traffic, at one request per round
12	 * trip, until the 100 req/s budget is gone. Canonical form is the precondition
13	 * that leaves the loop with no fuel.
14	 *
15	 * What a caller must know:
16	 *
17	 * - **Canonicalise before comparing or storing.** The stored form is canonical,
18	 *   so `field_version.sf_value`, the current value and an incoming value are
19	 *   all in the same spelling by construction.
20	 * - **`''` and `NULL` are one thing, stored `NULL`** (design 7.3). An
21	 *   empty-or-whitespace-only string returns `null`, so "cleared" has one
22	 *   representation rather than two that compare as different.
23	 * - **An unknown field name raises {@link WebhookRejected} with status 400.**
24	 *   That is the 400/500 pair of design 5: an unknown *field name* is a payload
25	 *   that will never work, so retrying cannot help, while a *value* we fail to
26	 *   canonicalise is our bug and earns a 500 and a retry.
27	 * - Nothing here is caught in order to continue quietly. The one failure this
28	 *   module can have — being handed a value it has no rule for — is surfaced as
29	 *   an error, because a silently mis-canonicalised value is exactly the
30	 *   divergence the module is here to prevent.
31	 */
32	
33	import { STATUS_VOCABULARY, fieldSpec } from "./fields.js";
34	import type { ObjectType } from "./types.js";
35	import { WebhookRejected } from "./types.js";
36	
37	/**
38	 * Reduce one raw field value to the one spelling comparisons use.
39	 *
40	 * @param objectType the record kind the field belongs to.
41	 * @param field the field name, as it arrived in the payload.
42	 * @param raw the value as it arrived, un-normalised. `null` means cleared.
43	 * @returns the canonical value, or `null` for a cleared or empty value.
44	 * @throws {WebhookRejected} status 400, reason `unknown-field`, when the object
45	 *   type has no such field.
46	 */
47	export function canonicalise(
48	  objectType: ObjectType,
49	  field: string,
50	  raw: string | null,
51	): string | null {
52	  const spec = fieldSpec(objectType, field);
53	  if (spec === undefined) {
54	    // Checked before the value, and before the null shortcut below: it is the
55	    // *name* that makes this payload unusable, so a null value must not turn a
56	    // 400 into a quiet `null`. 400 and not 500 because no retry can help
57	    // (design 5, "400 versus 500").
58	    throw new WebhookRejected(
59	      `unknown field ${JSON.stringify(field)} on ${objectType}`,
60	      400,
61	      "unknown-field",
62	    );
63	  }
64	
65	  if (raw === null) return null;
66	
67	  const text = collapseText(raw);
68	  // design 7.3: `''` and `NULL` are one thing, stored `NULL`. Two
69	  // representations of "cleared" would compare as a disagreement and so would
70	  // owe a repair write (design 8.3) forever.
71	  if (text === "") return null;
72	
73	  switch (spec.kind) {
74	    case "text":
75	      return text;
76	
77	    case "email":
78	      // Lowercased *whole*, local part included. Strictly, a mail server may
79	      // treat the local part as case-sensitive; the design chooses one
80	      // spelling anyway, because two spellings of one address would read as a
81	      // disagreement and owe a repair write forever (design 7.3, 8.3).
82	      return text.toLowerCase();
83	
84	    case "id":
85	      // Our own UUIDs, lowercase hex (design 7.3). Both sides hand this value
86	      // back to us, and a hex digit's case must not make a link look broken.
87	      return text.toLowerCase();
88	
89	    case "phone":
90	      return canonicalisePhone(text);
91	
92	    case "picklist": {
93	      // Looked up by the lowercased value, so "On Hold", "on-hold" and
94	      // "ONHOLD" are one status (design 7.3).
95	      const mapped = STATUS_VOCABULARY[text.toLowerCase()];
96	      if (mapped !== undefined) return mapped;
97	      // An unknown value is *data we pass through*, not an error. We were
98	      // given the agreed vocabulary, not a promise that it is exhaustive, and
99	      // a 400 here would discard a real edit forever. The consequence — every
100	      // echo of a value we cannot normalise reading as a disagreement — is
101	      // bounded by the repair breaker of design 9.4, which stops the argument
102	      // at 5 repairs an hour and marks the field contested.
103	      return text;
104	    }
105	
106	    default: {
107	      // Exhaustiveness, deliberately noisy: a tenth field (assumption A14) is
108	      // configuration, but a *new kind* is code, and the design is explicit
109	      // that a value we cannot canonicalise is our bug — a 500 and a retry,
110	      // never a value passed through in whatever spelling it arrived in.
111	      throw new WebhookRejected(
112	        `no canonical rule for kind ${JSON.stringify(spec.kind)} (field ${field})`,
113	        500,
114	        "canonicalise-failed",
115	      );
116	    }
117	  }
118	}
119	
120	/**
121	 * The phone rule of design 7.3: E.164-ish where the value parses, and digits
122	 * with a leading `+` where it does not.
123	 *
124	 * The design says "E.164 by the contact's country". A real implementation
125	 * would hand this to a library with a country hint; this demo does the part
126	 * that the loop rule actually depends on — throwing away every spelling
127	 * difference — and keeps the design's two branches visible, because the
128	 * branch a value lands in is what the parse-failure counter counts.
129	 */
130	function canonicalisePhone(text: string): string {
131	  // Everything that is not a digit goes, including the leading `+`, which is
132	  // then put back unconditionally: "+91 98765 43210" and "919876543210" are
133	  // one number, and a difference in how Salesforce chose to punctuate it must
134	  // not read as a change (design 7.3).
135	  const digits = text.replace(/\D/gu, "");
136	
137	  if (digits.length >= 10) {
138	    // Long enough to be a full national or international number, so this is
139	    // the E.164-ish form.
140	    return `+${digits}`;
141	  }
142	
143	  // The parse-failure branch. The design raises the parse-failure counter
144	  // here (design 7.3) and *still stores the value*: a short or malformed
145	  // number is Salesforce's data, and rejecting the event would discard a real
146	  // edit forever, which the 400/500 pair of design 5 forbids for a value we
147	  // merely failed to parse. There is no counter in this demo's store, so the
148	  // branch is kept separate and named rather than collapsed into the one
149	  // above — the two produce the same string today, and only one of them is a
150	  // number we believe in.
151	  return `+${digits}`;
152	}
153	
154	/**
155	 * The shared text rule of design 7.3: Unicode NFC, trimmed, internal
156	 * whitespace runs collapsed to one space.
157	 *
158	 * Every other kind is this plus one step, which is why it is one function:
159	 * `email` is this lowercased, `picklist` is this looked up, and a `phone` that
160	 * fails to parse is this reduced to digits.
161	 */
162	function collapseText(raw: string): string {
163	  // NFC first: trimming and collapsing are defined on code points, and the
164	  // decomposed and composed spellings of one accented name must not survive as
165	  // two values (design 7.3).
166	  return raw.normalize("NFC").trim().replace(/\s+/gu, " ");
167	}

14	 *
15	 * What a caller must know:
16	 *
17	 * - **Canonicalise before comparing or storing.** The stored form is canonical,
18	 *   so `field_version.sf_value`, the current value and an incoming value are
19	 *   all in the same spelling by construction.
20	 * - **`''` and `NULL` are one thing, stored `NULL`** (design 7.3). An
21	 *   empty-or-whitespace-only string returns `null`, so "cleared" has one
22	 *   representation rather than two that compare as different.
23	 * - **An unknown field name raises {@link WebhookRejected} with status 400.**
24	 *   That is the 400/500 pair of design 5: an unknown *field name* is a payload
25	 *   that will never work, so retrying cannot help, while a *value* we fail to
26	 *   canonicalise is our bug and earns a 500 and a retry.
27	 * - Nothing here is caught in order to continue quietly. The one failure this
28	 *   module can have — being handed a value it has no rule for — is surfaced as
29	 *   an error, because a silently mis-canonicalised value is exactly the
30	 *   divergence the module is here to prevent.
31	 */
32	
33	import { STATUS_VOCABULARY, fieldSpec } from "./fields.js";
34	import type { ObjectType } from "./types.js";
35	import { WebhookRejected } from "./types.js";
36	
37	/**
38	 * Reduce one raw field value to the one spelling comparisons use.
39	 *
40	 * @param objectType the record kind the field belongs to.
41	 * @param field the field name, as it arrived in the payload.
42	 * @param raw the value as it arrived, un-normalised. `null` means cleared.
43	 * @returns the canonical value, or `null` for a cleared or empty value.
44	 * @throws {WebhookRejected} status 400, reason `unknown-field`, when the object
45	 *   type has no such field.
46	 */
47	export function canonicalise(
48	  objectType: ObjectType,
49	  field: string,
50	  raw: string | null,
51	): string | null {
52	  const spec = fieldSpec(objectType, field);
53	  if (spec === undefined) {
54	    // Checked before the value, and before the null shortcut below: it is the
55	    // *name* that makes this payload unusable, so a null value must not turn a
56	    // 400 into a quiet `null`. 400 and not 500 because no retry can help
57	    // (design 5, "400 versus 500").
58	    throw new WebhookRejected(
59	      `unknown field ${JSON.stringify(field)} on ${objectType}`,
60	      400,
61	      "unknown-field",
62	    );
63	  }
64	
65	  if (raw === null) return null;
66	
67	  const text = collapseText(raw);
68	  // design 7.3: `''` and `NULL` are one thing, stored `NULL`. Two
69	  // representations of "cleared" would compare as a disagreement and so would
70	  // owe a repair write (design 8.3) forever.
71	  if (text === "") return null;
72	
73	  switch (spec.kind) {
74	    case "text":
75	      return text;
76	
77	    case "email":
78	      // Lowercased *whole*, local part included. Strictly, a mail server may
79	      // treat the local part as case-sensitive; the design chooses one
80	      // spelling anyway, because two spellings of one address would read as a
81	      // disagreement and owe a repair write forever (design 7.3, 8.3).
82	      return text.toLowerCase();
83	
84	    case "id":
85	      // Our own UUIDs, lowercase hex (design 7.3). Both sides hand this value
86	      // back to us, and a hex digit's case must not make a link look broken.
87	      return text.toLowerCase();
88	
89	    case "phone":
90	      return canonicalisePhone(text);
91	
92	    case "picklist": {
93	      // Looked up by the lowercased value, so "On Hold", "on-hold" and
94	      // "ONHOLD" are one status (design 7.3).
95	      const mapped = STATUS_VOCABULARY[text.toLowerCase()];
96	      if (mapped !== undefined) return mapped;
97	      // An unknown value is *data we pass through*, not an error. We were
98	      // given the agreed vocabulary, not a promise that it is exhaustive, and
99	      // a 400 here would discard a real edit forever. The consequence — every
100	      // echo of a value we cannot normalise reading as a disagreement — is
101	      // bounded by the repair breaker of design 9.4, which stops the argument
102	      // at 5 repairs an hour and marks the field contested.
103	      return text;
104	    }
105	
106	    default: {
107	      // Exhaustiveness, deliberately noisy: a tenth field (assumption A14) is
108	      // configuration, but a *new kind* is code, and the design is explicit
109	      // that a value we cannot canonicalise is our bug — a 500 and a retry,
110	      // never a value passed through in whatever spelling it arrived in.
111	      throw new WebhookRejected(
112	        `no canonical rule for kind ${JSON.stringify(spec.kind)} (field ${field})`,
113	        500,
114	        "canonicalise-failed",
115	      );
116	    }
117	  }
118	}
119	
120	/**
121	 * The phone rule of design 7.3: E.164-ish where the value parses, and digits
122	 * with a leading `+` where it does not.
123	 *
124	 * The design says "E.164 by the contact's country". A real implementation
125	 * would hand this to a library with a country hint; this demo does the part
126	 * that the loop rule actually depends on — throwing away every spelling
127	 * difference — and keeps the design's two branches visible, because the
128	 * branch a value lands in is what the parse-failure counter counts.
129	 */
130	function canonicalisePhone(text: string): string {
131	  // Everything that is not a digit goes, including the leading `+`, which is
132	  // then put back unconditionally: "+91 98765 43210" and "919876543210" are
133	  // one number, and a difference in how Salesforce chose to punctuate it must
134	  // not read as a change (design 7.3).
135	  const digits = text.replace(/\D/gu, "");
136	
137	  if (digits.length >= 10) {
138	    // Long enough to be a full national or international number, so this is
139	    // the E.164-ish form.
140	    return `+${digits}`;
141	  }
142	
143	  // The parse-failure branch. The design raises the parse-failure counter
144	  // here (design 7.3) and *still stores the value*: a short or malformed
145	  // number is Salesforce's data, and rejecting the event would discard a real
146	  // edit forever, which the 400/500 pair of design 5 forbids for a value we
147	  // merely failed to parse. There is no counter in this demo's store, so the
148	  // branch is kept separate and named rather than collapsed into the one
149	  // above — the two produce the same string today, and only one of them is a
150	  // number we believe in.
151	  return `+${digits}`;
152	}
153	
154	/**
155	 * The shared text rule of design 7.3: Unicode NFC, trimmed, internal
156	 * whitespace runs collapsed to one space.
157	 *
158	 * Every other kind is this plus one step, which is why it is one function:
159	 * `email` is this lowercased, `picklist` is this looked up, and a `phone` that
160	 * fails to parse is this reduced to digits.
161	 */
162	function collapseText(raw: string): string {
163	  // NFC first: trimming and collapsing are defined on code points, and the
164	  // decomposed and composed spellings of one accented name must not survive as
165	  // two values (design 7.3).
166	  return raw.normalize("NFC").trim().replace(/\s+/gu, " ");
167	}

---

## Appendix E: what the demo substitutes for

The optional code in `src/` implements the rules above and runs on Node alone,
so three things the design assumes are stood in for. Each substitution is also
documented at the point it is made — `src/store/store.ts` carries this table in
its own module docstring — because a reviewer checking code against design
needs to know which guarantees are real and which are imitated.

| The design assumes | The demo uses | Faithful? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Postgres tables** | one JSON document on disk, keyed objects and arrays | yes |
| **`BEGIN` / `COMMIT`** | mutate a deep clone, then write the file atomically; a throw discards the clone | **yes**, for one process — which is what part 5 needs, since the duplicate claim and the apply must commit together |
| **durability across a restart** | `writeFileSync` to a temp path, then `renameSync`, which is atomic on POSIX | **yes** — the demo SIGKILLs a child process and the queued call is still there |
| **`SELECT … FOR UPDATE`** (the per-record lock) | nothing: one process, one transaction at a time | **imitated.** The demo cannot show that the lock serialises competing merges, because it has no concurrency |
| **`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`** | the `leaseOwner` / `leaseUntilMs` columns the design already carries | **yes** — the lease, and its reclaim after a sender dies, are real |
| **the partial unique index** (one pending row per field) | an explicit check in the enqueue path | imitated |
| **`LISTEN` / `NOTIFY`** | the demo calls the worker directly | imitated |
| **monthly partitions and pruning** | not implemented | absent — retention is a design concern, not a rule |
| **the live Salesforce record API** | a fake written for this repository, file-backed so it survives the restart, with levers for the four behaviours the rules depend on: it echoes every write, it can be unreachable, it can answer 429, and it can refuse a record's data | the second adapter at the seam (part 2) |
| **HTTPS to the webhook endpoint** | the handler is called in-process, with the signature still verified over the raw body | imitated — the rules live in the handler, not in the HTTP framing |
| **70 req/s** (part 6.4) | a deliberately low cap so the wait is visible, which the exercise permits. **The code enforces whatever cap it is given** | the enforcement is real, the number is not the design's |
| **a 30-second lease** (part 6.5) | a shorter one, for the same reason | as above |

Two of these are worth stating as limits rather than details. The demo **does
not** show the record-level lock doing its job, because proving that needs
concurrency it does not have; the lock is in the code and its contract is in
part 2, but the evidence here is the rules and the ordering, not the locking.
And the demo's echo fence is per **event** rather than per field, because
`applyChanges` takes one classification — strictly more conservative than the
design, since it can never mistake a real change for an echo.

## Appendix B: the overwrite race, traced

The race the captain asked to see. It is the hardest case in this design and
tracing it found a bug, so it gets its own appendix.

**Setup.** `phone` currently `+919000000000` (OLD), last observed from
Salesforce at 09:00:00. F = `+919000000111` (finance), S = `+919000000222`
(sales).

| # | Time | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 10:00:00.000 *(our clock)* | finance saves `phone = F` in the portal |
| 2 | 10:00:01.000 *(SF clock)* | sales sets `phone = S` in Salesforce |
| 3 | 10:00:05.000 | our call lands, writing **F** over S in Salesforce |
| 4 | 10:00:06.000 | the webhook for step 2 finally arrives |
| 5 | 10:00:07.000 | the echo of our step-3 write arrives |

**Step 1 — the portal save.**
```
order key (10:00:00.000, rank 0, pc_1) > (09:00:00, 1, evt_prev)   -> APPLIED
current := F ;  field_change += (OLD -> F, finance.user, applied)
(d) sf_value OLD <> current F                                      -> 1 outbound row
```

**Step 3 — our call lands.** The sender reads the current value at send time
(6.3) and sends F. Salesforce now holds F: **the sales edit has been
overwritten in Salesforce.** On the 2xx (6.3):
```
sf_value := F ,  sf_observed_at := 10:00:05.000
echo_fence(phone, hash(F))
```

**Step 4 — the sales webhook arrives**, `occurredAt 10:00:01.000`,
`changedBy sales.user`.
```
L2  not the integration user                                        -> not an echo
(a) 10:00:01.000 > sf_observed_at 10:00:05.000 ?  NO
    -> sf_value STAYS F. Our 10:00:05 write is later than the edit
       this webhook describes, so it is still the freshest thing we
       know about Salesforce's state.
(b) S <> sf_value F                                                 -> a real change
(c) (10:00:01.000, 1, evt_S) > (10:00:00.000, 0, pc_1)              -> APPLIED
    current := S ;  field_change += (F -> S, sales.user, 10:00:01, applied)
(d) sf_value F <> current S                                         -> REPAIR queued
```

**Step 5 — the echo of our own write arrives**, `occurredAt ~10:00:05.000`,
value F, `changedBy integration.user`.
```
L2  -> ECHO. sync_observation('echo'). Step (c) never runs.
(d) sf_value F <> current S -> a repair is already pending for this field;
    the partial unique index on outbound_change keeps it at one row.
```

**Step 6 — the repair sends.** Reads the current value, sends **S**. Salesforce
holds S. `sf_value := S`. Its own echo then makes `sf_value` equal the current
value and condition (d) goes false. Settled.

#### The result

```
portal:      phone = S  (sales, 10:00:01)
Salesforce:  phone = S
history:     OLD -> F  finance.user  10:00:00  applied
             F   -> S  sales.user    10:00:01  applied
```

**Both copies end on the sales value**, and the finance edit is on record with
its author rather than being silently discarded.

#### Why the echo cannot win on its later `occurredAt`

Because it is classified as an echo by `changedBy` **before** any order-key
comparison happens, so its 10:00:05 stamp is never compared — which is
load-bearing rather than tidy, since that stamp is later than the sales edit's
10:00:01 and would otherwise let our own write launder the value we sent back
over a newer edit from the other side.

#### The bug this trace found

Without step 3's `sf_value := F`, step 4(a) would have seen `10:00:01.000 >
09:00:00` and set `sf_value := S`. Condition (d) would then have compared S
against a current value of S, found them equal, and queued **no repair** —
leaving Salesforce holding F and the portal holding S, permanently, with every
metric green. The fix is one line in the sender, and the reason it was missing
is that I had been treating `sf_value` as "what Salesforce told us" when it has
to mean "what we believe Salesforce holds", and our own writes are part of that.

---

## Appendix C: interfaces, schema and the sequences

actor            text    NOT NULL,
  outcome          text    NOT NULL CHECK (outcome IN ('applied','superseded')),
  applied_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp(),
  PRIMARY KEY (seq, applied_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (applied_at);          -- monthly partitions

CREATE INDEX ON field_change (object_type, portal_id, field, occurred_at DESC);

CREATE TABLE sync_observation (
  object_type text, portal_id uuid, field text,
  observed_value text, occurred_at timestamptz(3),
  origin text, origin_event_id text, actor text,
  outcome text NOT NULL CHECK (outcome IN ('echo','confirmed')),
  observed_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp()
) PARTITION BY RANGE (observed_at);         -- monthly partitions, dropped at 90 days

-- inbound idempotency. Part 8.1.
CREATE TABLE inbound_event (
  event_id     text PRIMARY KEY,              -- Salesforce's eventId
  object_type  text NOT NULL,
  sf_id        text NOT NULL,
  occurred_at  timestamptz(3) NOT NULL,
  payload_hash bytea NOT NULL,                -- sha256 of the raw body
  outcome      text NOT NULL,                 -- applied | echo | superseded | partial | rejected
  received_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp()
);
CREATE INDEX ON inbound_event (received_at);  -- for the 30-day prune

-- the durable outbound queue. Part 6. This is what "pending calls survive a
-- restart" means concretely: these rows are committed with the edit itself.
CREATE TABLE outbound_change (
  id              bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  object_type     text NOT NULL,
  portal_id       uuid NOT NULL,
  field           text NOT NULL,
  reason          text NOT NULL,              -- 'portal-edit' | 'repair' | 'create' | 'recovery'
  occurred_at     timestamptz(3) NOT NULL,    -- order key of the change that created this row
  state           text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
                  -- pending | inflight | sent | failed
  attempts        int  NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  next_attempt_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp(),
  lease_owner     text,
  lease_until     timestamptz,
  last_error      text,
  created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp(),
  sent_at         timestamptz
);
CREATE INDEX ON outbound_change (state, next_attempt_at)
  WHERE state IN ('pending','inflight');      -- the claim query's only index
CREATE INDEX ON outbound_change (object_type, portal_id) WHERE state = 'pending';
CREATE INDEX ON outbound_change (object_type, portal_id, field, created_at)
  WHERE reason = 'repair';                    -- the repair breaker's count (9.4)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON outbound_change (object_type, portal_id, field)
  WHERE state = 'pending';                    -- at most one pending call per field

-- identity across the two systems. S5. A portal-created record has a
-- portal_id before it has an sf_id.
CREATE TABLE record_link (
  object_type text NOT NULL,
  portal_id   uuid NOT NULL,
  sf_id       text,                            -- null until Salesforce assigns one
  linked_at   timestamptz,
  PRIMARY KEY (object_type, portal_id)
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON record_link (object_type, sf_id) WHERE sf_id IS NOT NULL;

-- "we just wrote this to Salesforce; expect to hear about it". Part 9, rule L3.
CREATE TABLE echo_fence (
  object_type text NOT NULL, portal_id uuid NOT NULL, field text NOT NULL,
  value_hash  bytea NOT NULL,                  -- sha256 of the canonical value we sent
  sent_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp(),
  expires_at  timestamptz NOT NULL,            -- sent_at + 15 minutes
  PRIMARY KEY (object_type, portal_id, field, value_hash)
);

-- how far through Salesforce's own change history we are confident. Part 10.
CREATE TABLE sync_watermark (
  object_type   text PRIMARY KEY,
  system_modstamp timestamptz NOT NULL,        -- highest SystemModstamp we have seen (A4)
  updated_at    timestamptz NOT NULL
);
```

  next_attempt_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp(),

  WHERE state = 'pending';                    -- at most one pending call per field

-- portal_id before it has an sf_id.
CREATE TABLE record_link (
  object_type text NOT NULL,
  portal_id   uuid NOT NULL,
  sf_id       text,                            -- null until Salesforce assigns one
  linked_at   timestamptz,
  PRIMARY KEY (object_type, portal_id)
);

CREATE TABLE echo_fence (
  object_type text NOT NULL, portal_id uuid NOT NULL, field text NOT NULL,
  value_hash  bytea NOT NULL,                  -- sha256 of the canonical value we sent
  sent_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp(),
  expires_at  timestamptz NOT NULL,            -- sent_at + 15 minutes
  PRIMARY KEY (object_type, portal_id, field, value_hash)

```
every tick (on NOTIFY, or every 1 second as a fallback):

      WHERE state='inflight' AND lease_until < clock_timestamp();

  2. if the circuit breaker is open, probe instead of claiming   (6.5)

  3. claim a batch, whole records at a time           (6.3)
     WITH due AS (

         FROM outbound_change
        WHERE state='pending' AND next_attempt_at <= clock_timestamp()
        GROUP BY object_type, portal_id
        ORDER BY due                      -- oldest-due record first: no starvation
        LIMIT 200

        WHERE o.state='pending' AND o.next_attempt_at <= clock_timestamp()
        FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED

            attempts = o.attempts + 1
       FROM picked p WHERE o.id = p.id

  5. for each group: read the CURRENT values of those fields, build one call   (6.3)
  6. governor.acquire(1 token)  -- every request, retries included            (6.5)
  7. send; settle the whole group by the outcome                              (6.7)

Part 10.3. The sweep must finish before the drain starts.

```
1. the breaker's probe succeeds -> the link is back
2. HOLD the outbound drain
3. for each object type, page through:
      SELECT Id, <fields>, SystemModstamp FROM {Type}
       WHERE SystemModstamp > :watermark ORDER BY SystemModstamp      (A4)

   with occurred_at = its SystemModstamp, origin = salesforce
4. advance sync_watermark to the highest SystemModstamp fully applied,
   after each page -> a crash resumes from the page boundary, and a
   small re-read overlap is harmless because applying an observation
   twice is a no-op (strict > in 7.2)
5. RELEASE the drain, at half rate, ramping (part 6.5)
```

content.content:
### F.5 The inbound path's four properties

**Why the duplicate claim and the apply must share one transaction.** A7 promises
redelivery only until we answer 200. Claim the `eventId` in its own transaction,
crash before applying, and the event is marked processed but never applied — and
Salesforce will never send it again. The edit is then lost with no record that it
existed, which is the exact failure class this design is about. It is the most
important line in the path.

**Why no network call inside the transaction.** A Salesforce call inside the
apply would hold record locks for the duration of someone else's outage, turning
a Salesforce incident into a Postgres incident. Keeping the transaction local
holds the endpoint's p99 at 200 ms and makes the inbound side independent of
Salesforce's availability — which is also what lets the 6-hour outage leave the
portal fully operational.

**Why value equality is checked before the order key.** Two reasons, and the
second is the load-bearing one. (1) `field_change` is the client's record of edits
that *changed* something; a re-save of the value already held is not one, and
filling permanent history with no-op rows makes "who changed the city" harder to
answer. (2) It must not restamp the order key: if a no-op re-save advanced the
stamp, it would take ownership of the field from a genuine edit, so a later real
edit from the other side could lose to someone who re-submitted a value they
never changed. This is a third layer of idempotence beneath the duplicate table
and the strict `>`, and the strict `>` remains the backstop that matters, because
it is what handles a *different* value arriving with an older stamp.

**Why case (c) is narrowed to the integration user.** Deferring with a 503
whenever *any* create is in flight would delay legitimate Salesforce creates by
5 s most of the time at A1's rate, to fix a race that only ever involves our own
writes. Treating (c) as (b) instead would mint a second local record for one real
contact. The narrow condition is what makes the cheap answer safe.

**400 versus 500.** A 400 discards the event forever, so the line has to be
exact: an unknown *field name* is a contract violation and earns a 400; a *value*
we failed to canonicalise is our bug, and it earns a 500 and a retry so the event
survives until we fix the canonicaliser.

whenever *any* create is in flight would delay legitimate Salesforce creates by
5 s most of the time at A1's rate, to fix a race that only ever involves our own
writes. Treating (c) as (b) instead would mint a second local record for one real
contact. The narrow condition is what makes the cheap answer safe.

**400 versus 500.** A 400 discards the event forever, so the line has to be
exact: an unknown *field name* is a contract violation and earns a 400; a *value*
we failed to canonicalise is our bug, and it earns a 500 and a retry so the event
survives until we fix the canonicaliser.

### F.6 The cap, the breaker, and reading the value late

# Two-way sync of customer and contact records

Tequity Round 1 exercise. The client runs sales in Salesforce and finance /
customer-success in a portal Tequity built on Postgres. The same customers and
contacts live in both systems and have to stay in two-way sync, with every
field's history kept.

## What is in this repository

| Path | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `docs/design.md` | **The design document. Start here.** The exercise's 12-part outline, assumptions first. It carries every rule, interface and number, and nothing else. |
| `docs/design-appendix.md` | The working behind the design, for checking a decision rather than building from it: A the brief's scenario traced, B the hardest race, C interfaces/schema/sequences, D each assumption's consequence and the alternatives rejected, E what the demo substitutes for, F the argument behind every rule, by section. |
| `CONTEXT.md` | Glossary. The project's domain vocabulary, fixed before the design leans on it. |
| `docs/adr/` | Decision records for the three choices that are expensive to reverse. |
| `src/`, `package.json` | The optional demo. TypeScript on Node 20+, a fake Salesforce, no external services. |

## Reading order

1. `docs/design.md` part 1 — assumptions and the questions I would have asked.
2. `docs/design.md` part 2 — the systems, who calls whom, the network seam.
3. `docs/design.md` parts 7-10 — the four rules: same-record conflict,
   duplicates and out-of-order, loop termination, and the 6-hour outage with
   the arithmetic.
4. `docs/design-appendix.md` appendix A — the exercise's own worked scenario
   (phone in Salesforce, city in the portal) traced through every rule, and
   appendix B — the overwrite race, which is where tracing found a real bug.
   Appendix F holds the reasoning behind each rule the design document states.

## Running the demo

```bash
npm install
npm run demo     # the six scenarios, with printed output
npm test         # the unit tests at the rule seams
```

Node 20 or newer. No network, no services, no credentials — a fake Salesforce
written for this repository stands in for the real one, and a JSON document on
disk stands in for Postgres. `docs/design-appendix.md` appendix E lists every
substitution and says which guarantees are real and which are imitated.

The demo runs six scenarios. Four are the checks the exercise names — a
duplicate webhook, an older event arriving after a newer one, our own update
coming back as a webhook and not being sent again, and a pending call still
present after a `SIGKILL` while the fake Salesforce is down — plus the brief's
own phone-and-city acceptance scenario and the rate cap. Each names the design
section it exercises, and a failed check exits non-zero rather than printing
"FAIL" and carrying on.

## Commit history

The commits are the record of how the design developed and are deliberately
not squashed. Each message says what was decided and why.

# Customer and contact sync

The one context in this repository: keeping the client's customer and contact
records consistent between Salesforce and the Tequity portal, in both
directions, without losing the record of who changed what and when.

## Language

### The records

**Record**:
One customer or one contact. The thing that exists in both Salesforce and the
portal and has to agree.
_Avoid_: entity, object, row.

**Customer**:
An organisation the client sells to. Has a name, a status and an owner.
_Avoid_: account, client, company.

**Contact**:
A person at a customer. Has a full name, phone, email, city, owner and the
customer they belong to.
_Avoid_: person, lead, user.

**Field**:
One named, separately syncable value on a record, such as a contact's city.
The field, not the record, is the unit that conflicts and the unit that carries
history.

### What happens to them

**Edit**:
One human action: a sales user saving in Salesforce, or a finance user saving
the portal form. An edit touches one or more fields.
_Avoid_: update, modification.

**Change**:
One field moving to one new value, attributed to one actor at one time. An
edit of three fields is three changes. Changes, not edits, are what the sync
reasons about.
_Avoid_: delta, event, patch.

**Origin**:
The system an edit was made in: Salesforce or the portal. Every change carries
its origin for the rest of its life.
_Avoid_: source, side, direction.

**Actor**:
The identified human or integration account that made an edit. Part of the
history the client is paying for, not metadata.
_Avoid_: user, author, editor.

### Deciding what is true

**Order key**:
The comparable value that decides which of two changes to the same field is
the later one. Two changes to one field are always comparable, and the
comparison gives the same answer wherever it is made.
_Avoid_: version, timestamp, sequence number.

content.content:
**Current value**:
The value of a field that the portal shows and that we are willing to defend
as correct: the value of the change with the highest order key for that field.
_Avoid_: latest value, truth, master value.

**Superseded change**:
A real change that lost the order-key comparison. It never becomes a current
value, and it is kept with its actor and time, because the client asked for the
fact of the earlier edit to stay on record.
_Avoid_: stale change, rejected change, discarded change.

**Canonical form**:
The single spelling of a value that comparisons use, so that two systems
agreeing on a value never look like they disagree. "+91 98765 43210" and
"+919876543210" have one canonical form.
_Avoid_: normalised value, cleaned value.

### Keeping the two sides apart

**Echo**:
A webhook describing a change we ourselves made in Salesforce moments earlier.
An echo is a genuine Salesforce notification, not a duplicate, and it carries
no new information.
_Avoid_: loopback, reflection, bounce.

**Repair write**:
An outbound call we send because we learned that Salesforce holds a value our
rules do not accept. It carries our current value and exists to end a
disagreement we detected rather than to publish a new edit.
_Avoid_: correction, reconciliation, force push.

**Integration user**:
The single Salesforce login every call of ours is made as. Its only purpose is
to make our own changes recognisable when Salesforce describes them back to us.
_Avoid_: service account, API user, bot.

**Record link**:
The pairing between a record's Salesforce identifier and its portal
identifier. A record created in the portal has a portal identifier before it
has a Salesforce one.
_Avoid_: mapping, id map, cross-reference.

**Watermark**:
The point in Salesforce's own change history up to which we are confident we
have seen everything. What recovery after an outage starts from.
_Avoid_: checkpoint, cursor, offset.

input.message:
Read-only review of `fm/tequity-sync-r1` in `/Users/dushyantjoshi/dushyant-joshi-workspace/projects/.treehouse/tequity-two-way-sync-653ea9/1/tequity-two-way-sync`.

**Fixed point:** `main` (3129b47) — you named the branch-vs-main comparison; `git merge-base HEAD main` equals main's tip, so `git diff main...HEAD` is the whole branch: 36 commits, 43 files, 8,917 insertions, working tree clean. **Spec source:** the `## Captain's intent` section of `/Users/dushyantjoshi/dushyant-joshi-workspace/data/tequity-sync-r1/brief.md`, with `docs/design.md` + `docs/design-appendix.md` as the stated rule source. **Standards source:** `docs/demo-code-conventions.md` (the repo's own recorded requirements) plus `CONTEXT.md`'s vocabulary, plus the smell baseline. Ran the two passes sequentially, notes kept separate. I did not re-run `npm test`/`npm run demo`; one finding was confirmed with a throwaway script against `dist/`.

## Standards

**Hard violation**

1. `src/outbound/worker.ts:303-316` + `:456-469` — a store failure is reported as an endpoint failure. `tx.linkSfId` (line 310) raises `StoreReadError`/`StoreWriteError` *inside* the send try-block, so the catch at 314 hands it to `settleFailure`'s fallback branch, which increments `consecutiveEndpointFailures` (can open the circuit breaker), returns `"endpoint-failure"` to the caller, and reports the real cause only via `process.emitWarning`. `docs/demo-code-conventions.md` ("Error handling"): "Store read and write failures are surfaced, never swallowed … the error visible to the caller." Work is preserved, so no data loss — but the caller is told the wrong thing and a disk problem can trip the Salesforce breaker.

**Judgement calls**

2. `src/store/store.ts:376-382` — `catch (error) { throw error; }` neither handles, translates, nor records; rollback is achieved by discarding the clone, not by the catch. The convention's three permitted shapes don't include a pure rethrow, and the comment implies the catch does the rollback.
3. `src/inbound/validate.ts:62-67` — unreachable catch: `Buffer.from(<string>, "hex")` does not throw on non-hex input (it silently drops invalid bytes), so the `SignatureInvalid` translation never runs and the comment's "rather than allowed to propagate as a TypeError" is wrong for string input. Behaviour is still correct via the length/`timingSafeEqual` check. Relevant to the captain's "error handling is real, not decorative" ask.
4. `src/outbound/worker.ts:294` — `row.lastError = "nothing owed: …"` stores a *success* note in the error column; anyone querying `last_error` for trouble finds routine skips.
5. Duplicated Code — `src/domain/merge.ts:176-186`, `:202-212`, `:233-243`: three ten-line `tx.appendObservation({...})` literals differing only in `outcome`. `src/outbound/worker.ts:411-418`, `:428-435`, `:460-467`: three `settle(batch, row => …)` bodies; the last two are identical but for the `lastError` string.
6. Data Clumps / Primitive Obsession — `(objectType, portalId, field)` travels as three separate params through ~15 signatures (`store.ts:122,255,300`, `merge.ts` helpers, `schema.ts:183`); a `FieldRef` wants to be born. And `sfValue: string | null | undefined` (`merge.ts:342`, `worker.ts:376`) encodes three distinct domain states — never learned / known-empty / known-value — as a bare union, which is exactly where the `IS DISTINCT FROM` subtlety lives.
7. Speculative Generality / dead code — `src/inbound/endpoint.ts:276` `ACCEPTED_OBJECT_TYPES` is exported "for the demo's printed output" with zero references anywhere; `src/salesforce/fake.ts:154-158` `rejectWritesTo` has no caller in `src/` or the tests, though the fake's module docstring advertises refusing a record's data as one of the four behaviours it exists to provide.
8. `src/store/store.ts:122-128`, `:277-287` — `getFieldVersion`, `findLinkBySfId`, `findLinkByPortalId` have no TSDoc, against "Every exported function has a TSDoc block" (they are public methods of an exported class; the names are self-describing, which is why this is a judgement call).

**Passing plainly:** no empty catch blocks anywhere (all 14 catches inspected); module and exported-function docstrings are otherwise complete; the four rule sites each carry a why-comment citing a design section, as the convention demands; `CONTEXT.md`'s vocabulary and its `_Avoid_` lists are honoured in identifiers (`echo`, `superseded`, `canonical`, `currentValueOf`, `INTEGRATION_USER`, `watermarks`), with `row`/`version` used only where `docs/design-appendix.md` C.2's own DDL uses them, so the repo overrides the smell.

## Spec

Axis 1 (code↔design rule-for-rule) first, since that is the priority.

**Hard divergences**

1. `src/inbound/endpoint.ts:186-201` — **design 5 case (c)'s 60-second bound is dead code, and the defer is unbounded.** `createRecord` (`src/store/store.ts:92-97`) sets `linkedAtMs` only when `sfId !== null`, so for exactly the rows this branch looks for (`sfId === null`) it is always `undefined`; line 191 then computes `waitedMs = nowMs() - (undefined ?? nowMs())`, which is always `0`. Design 5 says "After 60 s, log loudly and treat as (b)". Verified: delivering an integration-user webhook for an unknown `recordId` while any portal-created record is unlinked returns `503 create-echo-before-link` at now, at +10 minutes and at +10 days. Failure scenario: a portal-created record whose create permanently failed (`state='failed'`) leaves `sfId = null` forever, and because line 187-189 matches *any* unlinked record of that object type, every subsequent integration-user webhook for an unknown id of that type is refused forever instead of falling through to case (b). Fix is one field (a link/record creation time), not the rule.
2. `docs/design-appendix.md:469-479` (C.3 step (c)) — **the build sequence states a different branch order than the code implements.** C.3 has: echo → order-key → superseded → confirmed. The code (`src/domain/merge.ts:187-288`) and `docs/design.md:196-198` and `F.5` (`design-appendix.md:724-733`) all have: echo → value-already-equal (`confirmed`) → order-key → superseded. These are not equivalent: a change whose value equals the current value but whose key is strictly newer is a no-op `confirmed` in the code and an `applied` row with a restamped order key in C.3 — the exact restamping `F.5` and `merge.ts:214-231` argue must not happen. A teammate building from C.3 implements the wrong rule. This looks like `b304bcd` ("Record the value-equality rule in the design") updating the body but not the sequence.
3. `docs/design-appendix.md:352` — `sync_observation`'s `CHECK (outcome IN ('echo','confirmed'))` rejects the `restatement` rows the code writes (`src/domain/merge.ts:176-186`, `src/store/schema.ts:85`), which `docs/design.md:176` lists as one of the three observation outcomes. The DDL as published would raise a constraint violation on the first full-record restatement — i.e. on design 8.4's own traced hazard. Same family: line 363's `inbound_event.outcome` comment omits `restatement`, which `endpoint.ts:157-158` can store.
4. `src/inbound/endpoint.ts:122-129` — design 8.1's "A repeated `eventId` carrying a *different* `payload_hash` is a provider bug: first write wins, and this one **is** alerted." The code returns 200 and the comment says "this one DOES deserve an alert", but no alert is raised, while the three comparable sites all use `process.emitWarning` (`merge.ts:381`, `worker.ts:450`, `endpoint.ts:198`). The one case the design deliberately contrasts against "counted, not alerted" is silent.

**Judgement calls**

5. `src/domain/merge.ts:375` — repair-breaker threshold. Design 9.4 says "Above **5** repairs to one field in an hour, enqueue nothing more"; `repairsInLastHour(...) > 5` lets the 6th through and blocks the 7th, which `src/domain/merge.test.ts:415,428` codifies ("at five repairs the breaker has not tripped yet" / "above six repairs … nothing more is enqueued"). Either tighten to `>= 5` or restate the rule as "more than five".
6. `src/outbound/governor.ts:66` + `src/demo/world.ts:65` — design 6.4's decrease is `rate := max(5, rate / 2)`; the floor defaults to `Math.min(1, ceiling)` and the demo passes `floorPerSecond: 1`. The design's `5` appears nowhere in the code, and the floor is the one governor constant Appendix E's substitution table (`design-appendix.md:617-618`, which does record the ceiling and the lease) does not mention.
7. `src/outbound/worker.ts:439-469` and `src/salesforce/client.ts` — design 6.5's settle table has six rows; the code implements four. There is no auth error type, so `401`/`403` ("pending, attempts restored, **page, stop the sender** — else the queue burns into `failed`") lands in the unexpected-error fallback: work is kept, but nothing stops the sender, and the fake has no lever for it.
8. `src/inbound/endpoint.ts:233-255` — `classifyEcho` *consumes* a matching fence even when the event is then classified as not-an-echo (match on 1 of 2 fields → fence gone, change applied as real). Appendix E records the per-event-rather-than-per-field simplification and calls it "strictly more conservative", which is true for classification but not for fence lifetime: with A6 false, a multi-field webhook burns L3's protection for the field it did match. L1 still terminates the loop, so this costs a repair call rather than correctness.
9. `src/outbound/worker.ts:287-297` — the claim-time "nothing-owed" skip marks the row `sent` without a request and cites "Design 10.3's claim-time filter", but 10.3 (`design.md:507`) and F.10 (`design-appendix.md:914`) say the queued row **sends** the current value as a no-op. Strictly better behaviour, not the stated rule, and it slightly undercuts 10.4's call counts.
10. `src/inbound/endpoint.ts:258-273` — `summarise` records a confirmed-only event as `"applied"`, directly under a comment about recording outcomes "honestly rather than rounding". No `EventOutcome` member covers it.
11. `src/outbound/worker.ts:324-342` vs `:383-388` — a create sends every field (`planCall` fills all of `fieldNames`) but records `sf_value` and an echo fence only for the batch's owed rows, where design 6.3 says the sender sets `sf_value` to "what it sent". Self-correcting (an unknown `sf_value` is conservative in the safe direction), so cost is at most one redundant call.

**Axis 2 — the four named checks plus the brief's scenario: all present and all actually assert the property.** `src/demo/scenarios/duplicate.ts` (byte-identical redelivery, *and* a replay with the claim deleted to prove the strict `>` layer independently), `outOfOrder.ts` (newer first, older second; asserts superseded-with-actor-and-time *and* that no repair was queued), `loop.ts` (asserts the first write actually left before asserting that nothing follows, then re-runs it with L2 defeated and with Salesforce reformatting the value), `restart.ts` (real child process, real `SIGKILL`, Salesforce down, asserts rows survive as `pending` with attempts restored, then expired-lease reclaim and a full drain), `phoneAndCity.ts` (ends with the new phone *and* the finance city, with `oldValue`/actor/origin on every history row), `rateCap.ts` (12 records at a 4 req/s ceiling, timed against the cap's floor; 429 halves the rate, then asserts every row reached Salesforce and none was marked failed). The rate cap is enforced from one place (`governor.acquire`, one token per request including retries) as 6.4 requires.

**Axis 3 — the captain's code asks are met** beyond the Standards notes above: every module and every exported function carries a TSDoc block, the four rule seams carry why-comments citing design sections, and no catch is empty. The two decorative spots are items 2 and 3 of the Standards list, and the one catch that swallows something it should not surface to its caller is Standards item 1.

**Dangling section numbers:** every `design N.M` / `Appendix X` citation in `src/` resolves against the compressed document, including the four `9.1-9.4` blockquote labels — no dangling references in the code. The stale ones are all inside `docs/design-appendix.md`: `:502` cites `(6.6)` and `:531` cites `(6.7)`, which no longer exist (reclaim is 6.2, settle is 6.5); `:506` and `:530` cite `(6.5)` for the breaker probe and the governor, both now 6.4; `:550` cites `(part 6.5)` for resuming at half rate, now 6.4; `:321` cites `(part 6.4)` for "our own successful send moves `sf_value`", which is 6.3 (the code cites 6.3 correctly in `src/store/schema.ts:46`); `:29` cites "5.1 case (b)" where part 5 has no numbered subsections. Also `Appendix F` starts at `F.2` with no `F.1` — nothing cites it, so it is cosmetic.

**Coverage gap worth naming:** `src/inbound/endpoint.ts` is the only non-trivial module with no test file (113 tests cover merge, orderKey, canonical, store, worker, governor, validate), and it is where findings 1, 4, 8 and 10 all live. The brief asked for tests "at the rule seams", and L2/L3 classification and design 5's three resolve cases are rule seams.

**No scope creep found.** Everything in the diff traces to the brief or the design; the fake's unused `rejectWritesTo` lever and `ACCEPTED_OBJECT_TYPES` are dead rather than extra behaviour, and `watermarks`/`OutboundReason`'s `create`/`recovery` members mirror C.2's published schema.

**Counts — Standards: 8 findings (1 hard, 7 judgement). ## Standards

**Hard violation**

1. `src/outbound/worker.ts:303-316` + `:456-469` — a store failure is reported as an endpoint failure. `tx.linkSfId` (line 310) raises `StoreReadError`/`StoreWriteError` *inside* the send try-block, so the catch at 314 hands it to `settleFailure`'s fallback branch, which increments `consecutiveEndpointFailures` (can open the circuit breaker), returns `"endpoint-failure"` to the caller, and reports the real cause only via `process.emitWarning`. `docs/demo-code-conventions.md` ("Error handling"): "Store read and write failures are surfaced, never swallowed … the error visible to the caller." Work is preserved, so no data loss — but the caller is told the wrong thing and a disk problem can trip the Salesforce breaker.

**Judgement calls**

2. `src/store/store.ts:376-382` — `catch (error) { throw error; }` neither handles, translates, nor records; rollback is achieved by discarding the clone, not by the catch. The convention's three permitted shapes don't include a pure rethrow, and the comment implies the catch does the rollback.
3. `src/inbound/validate.ts:62-67` — unreachable catch: `Buffer.from(<string>, "hex")` does not throw on non-hex input (it silently drops invalid bytes), so the `SignatureInvalid` translation never runs and the comment's "rather than allowed to propagate as a TypeError" is wrong for string input. Behaviour is still correct via the length/`timingSafeEqual` check. Relevant to the captain's "error handling is real, not decorative" ask.
4. `src/outbound/worker.ts:294` — `row.lastError = "nothing owed: …"` stores a *success* note in the error column; anyone querying `last_error` for trouble finds routine skips.
5. Duplicated Code — `src/domain/merge.ts:176-186`, `:202-212`, `:233-243`: three ten-line `tx.appendObservation({...})` literals differing only in `outcome`. `src/outbound/worker.ts:411-418`, `:428-435`, `:460-467`: three `settle(batch, row => …)` bodies; the last two are identical but for the `lastError` string.
6. Data Clumps / Primitive Obsession — `(objectType, portalId, field)` travels as three separate params through ~15 signatures (`store.ts:122,255,300`, `merge.ts` helpers, `schema.ts:183`); a `FieldRef` wants to be born. And `sfValue: string | null | undefined` (`merge.ts:342`, `worker.ts:376`) encodes three distinct domain states — never learned / known-empty / known-value — as a bare union, which is exactly where the `IS DISTINCT FROM` subtlety lives.
7. Speculative Generality / dead code — `src/inbound/endpoint.ts:276` `ACCEPTED_OBJECT_TYPES` is exported "for the demo's printed output" with zero references anywhere; `src/salesforce/fake.ts:154-158` `rejectWritesTo` has no caller in `src/` or the tests, though the fake's module docstring advertises refusing a record's data as one of the four behaviours it exists to provide.
8. `src/store/store.ts:122-128`, `:277-287` — `getFieldVersion`, `findLinkBySfId`, `findLinkByPortalId` have no TSDoc, against "Every exported function has a TSDoc block" (they are public methods of an exported class; the names are self-describing, which is why this is a judgement call).

**Passing plainly:** no empty catch blocks anywhere (all 14 catches inspected); module and exported-function docstrings are otherwise complete; the four rule sites each carry a why-comment citing a design section, as the convention demands; `CONTEXT.md`'s vocabulary and its `_Avoid_` lists are honoured in identifiers (`echo`, `superseded`, `canonical`, `currentValueOf`, `INTEGRATION_USER`, `watermarks`), with `row`/`version` used only where `docs/design-appendix.md` C.2's own DDL uses them, so the repo overrides the smell.

## Spec

Axis 1 (code↔design rule-for-rule) first, since that is the priority.

**Hard divergences**

1. `src/inbound/endpoint.ts:186-201` — **design 5 case (c)'s 60-second bound is dead code, and the defer is unbounded.** `createRecord` (`src/store/store.ts:92-97`) sets `linkedAtMs` only when `sfId !== null`, so for exactly the rows this branch looks for (`sfId === null`) it is always `undefined`; line 191 then computes `waitedMs = nowMs() - (undefined ?? nowMs())`, which is always `0`. Design 5 says "After 60 s, log loudly and treat as (b)". Verified: delivering an integration-user webhook for an unknown `recordId` while any portal-created record is unlinked returns `503 create-echo-before-link` at now, at +10 minutes and at +10 days. Failure scenario: a portal-created record whose create permanently failed (`state='failed'`) leaves `sfId = null` forever, and because line 187-189 matches *any* unlinked record of that object type, every subsequent integration-user webhook for an unknown id of that type is refused forever instead of falling through to case (b). Fix is one field (a link/record creation time), not the rule.
2. `docs/design-appendix.md:469-479` (C.3 step (c)) — **the build sequence states a different branch order than the code implements.** C.3 has: echo → order-key → superseded → confirmed. The code (`src/domain/merge.ts:187-288`) and `docs/design.md:196-198` and `F.5` (`design-appendix.md:724-733`) all have: echo → value-already-equal (`confirmed`) → order-key → superseded. These are not equivalent: a change whose value equals the current value but whose key is strictly newer is a no-op `confirmed` in the code and an `applied` row with a restamped order key in C.3 — the exact restamping `F.5` and `merge.ts:214-231` argue must not happen. A teammate building from C.3 implements the wrong rule. This looks like `b304bcd` ("Record the value-equality rule in the design") updating the body but not the sequence.
3. `docs/design-appendix.md:352` — `sync_observation`'s `CHECK (outcome IN ('echo','confirmed'))` rejects the `restatement` rows the code writes (`src/domain/merge.ts:176-186`, `src/store/schema.ts:85`), which `docs/design.md:176` lists as one of the three observation outcomes. The DDL as published would raise a constraint violation on the first full-record restatement — i.e. on design 8.4's own traced hazard. Same family: line 363's `inbound_event.outcome` comment omits `restatement`, which `endpoint.ts:157-158` can store.
4. `src/inbound/endpoint.ts:122-129` — design 8.1's "A repeated `eventId` carrying a *different* `payload_hash` is a provider bug: first write wins, and this one **is** alerted." The code returns 200 and the comment says "this one DOES deserve an alert", but no alert is raised, while the three comparable sites all use `process.emitWarning` (`merge.ts:381`, `worker.ts:450`, `endpoint.ts:198`). The one case the design deliberately contrasts against "counted, not alerted" is silent.

**Judgement calls**

5. `src/domain/merge.ts:375` — repair-breaker threshold. Design 9.4 says "Above **5** repairs to one field in an hour, enqueue nothing more"; `repairsInLastHour(...) > 5` lets the 6th through and blocks the 7th, which `src/domain/merge.test.ts:415,428` codifies ("at five repairs the breaker has not tripped yet" / "above six repairs … nothing more is enqueued"). Either tighten to `>= 5` or restate the rule as "more than five".
6. `src/outbound/governor.ts:66` + `src/demo/world.ts:65` — design 6.4's decrease is `rate := max(5, rate / 2)`; the floor defaults to `Math.min(1, ceiling)` and the demo passes `floorPerSecond: 1`. The design's `5` appears nowhere in the code, and the floor is the one governor constant Appendix E's substitution table (`design-appendix.md:617-618`, which does record the ceiling and the lease) does not mention.
7. `src/outbound/worker.ts:439-469` and `src/salesforce/client.ts` — design 6.5's settle table has six rows; the code implements four. There is no auth error type, so `401`/`403` ("pending, attempts restored, **page, stop the sender** — else the queue burns into `failed`") lands in the unexpected-error fallback: work is kept, but nothing stops the sender, and the fake has no lever for it.
8. `src/inbound/endpoint.ts:233-255` — `classifyEcho` *consumes* a matching fence even when the event is then classified as not-an-echo (match on 1 of 2 fields → fence gone, change applied as real). Appendix E records the per-event-rather-than-per-field simplification and calls it "strictly more conservative", which is true for classification but not for fence lifetime: with A6 false, a multi-field webhook burns L3's protection for the field it did match. L1 still terminates the loop, so this costs a repair call rather than correctness.
9. `src/outbound/worker.ts:287-297` — the claim-time "nothing-owed" skip marks the row `sent` without a request and cites "Design 10.3's claim-time filter", but 10.3 (`design.md:507`) and F.10 (`design-appendix.md:914`) say the queued row **sends** the current value as a no-op. Strictly better behaviour, not the stated rule, and it slightly undercuts 10.4's call counts.
10. `src/inbound/endpoint.ts:258-273` — `summarise` records a confirmed-only event as `"applied"`, directly under a comment about recording outcomes "honestly rather than rounding". No `EventOutcome` member covers it.
11. `src/outbound/worker.ts:324-342` vs `:383-388` — a create sends every field (`planCall` fills all of `fieldNames`) but records `sf_value` and an echo fence only for the batch's owed rows, where design 6.3 says the sender sets `sf_value` to "what it sent". Self-correcting (an unknown `sf_value` is conservative in the safe direction), so cost is at most one redundant call.

**Axis 2 — the four named checks plus the brief's scenario: all present and all actually assert the property.** `src/demo/scenarios/duplicate.ts` (byte-identical redelivery, *and* a replay with the claim deleted to prove the strict `>` layer independently), `outOfOrder.ts` (newer first, older second; asserts superseded-with-actor-and-time *and* that no repair was queued), `loop.ts` (asserts the first write actually left before asserting that nothing follows, then re-runs it with L2 defeated and with Salesforce reformatting the value), `restart.ts` (real child process, real `SIGKILL`, Salesforce down, asserts rows survive as `pending` with attempts restored, then expired-lease reclaim and a full drain), `phoneAndCity.ts` (ends with the new phone *and* the finance city, with `oldValue`/actor/origin on every history row), `rateCap.ts` (12 records at a 4 req/s ceiling, timed against the cap's floor; 429 halves the rate, then asserts every row reached Salesforce and none was marked failed). The rate cap is enforced from one place (`governor.acquire`, one token per request including retries) as 6.4 requires.

**Axis 3 — the captain's code asks are met** beyond the Standards notes above: every module and every exported function carries a TSDoc block, the four rule seams carry why-comments citing design sections, and no catch is empty. The two decorative spots are items 2 and 3 of the Standards list, and the one catch that swallows something it should not surface to its caller is Standards item 1.

**Dangling section numbers:** every `design N.M` / `Appendix X` citation in `src/` resolves against the compressed document, including the four `9.1-9.4` blockquote labels — no dangling references in the code. The stale ones are all inside `docs/design-appendix.md`: `:502` cites `(6.6)` and `:531` cites `(6.7)`, which no longer exist (reclaim is 6.2, settle is 6.5); `:506` and `:530` cite `(6.5)` for the breaker probe and the governor, both now 6.4; `:550` cites `(part 6.5)` for resuming at half rate, now 6.4; `:321` cites `(part 6.4)` for "our own successful send moves `sf_value`", which is 6.3 (the code cites 6.3 correctly in `src/store/schema.ts:46`); `:29` cites "5.1 case (b)" where part 5 has no numbered subsections. Also `Appendix F` starts at `F.2` with no `F.1` — nothing cites it, so it is cosmetic.

**Coverage gap worth naming:** `src/inbound/endpoint.ts` is the only non-trivial module with no test file (113 tests cover merge, orderKey, canonical, store, worker, governor, validate), and it is where findings 1, 4, 8 and 10 all live. The brief asked for tests "at the rule seams", and L2/L3 classification and design 5's three resolve cases are rule seams.

**No scope creep found.** Everything in the diff traces to the brief or the design; the fake's unused `rejectWritesTo` lever and `ACCEPTED_OBJECT_TYPES` are dead rather than extra behaviour, and `watermarks`/`OutboundReason`'s `create`/`recovery` members mirror C.2's published schema.
